chapters.n: Second Samuel picks up right where 1 Samuel ends. Saul has just died in battle, and David, back from rescuing his people’s families from Amalekite raiders, waits in Ziklag, the Philistine town where he had been living as an outlaw.

f.g: A town in the Negev given to David by Achish, the Philistine king of Gath (1 Samuel 27:6).

chapters.n: A messenger arrives showing every sign of mourning — torn clothes and dirt on his head. He bows low before David, as if already treating him as the new king.

f.g: Rent = torn. Tearing one’s garments and putting dust on the head were customary signs of grief or disaster.
Bowed down with his face to the ground as a sign of honor.

chapters.n: David asks where he has come from, and the man says he escaped from Israel’s army camp — a hint that the news is very bad.

f.g: Whence = from where.

chapters.n: The news is the worst possible: Israel has been routed, many are dead, and both King Saul and Jonathan, David’s dearest friend, have fallen.

f.w: Saul and Jonathan his son are dead

chapters.n: David does not simply accept the report. He presses the young man for proof, perhaps already sensing something is off in his story.
The Amalekite says he “happened by chance” on Mount Gilboa and found Saul leaning on his spear with enemy chariots closing in. His account differs from 1 Samuel 31, where Saul falls on his own sword.

f.g: A ridge at the eastern edge of the Jezreel Valley in northern Israel, where Saul made his last stand.

chapters.n: In his story, the wounded Saul spotted him and called out, and he answered as a willing servant.
He admits he is an Amalekite — a member of the very people Saul had been commanded to destroy, and whom David had just been fighting. The irony would not be lost on readers.
According to the man, Saul begged to be killed because he was in agony yet still alive.

f.g: The Hebrew word is rare; it may mean a cramp, dizziness, or the agony of a mortal wound.

chapters.n: He claims he finished Saul off and brought the king’s crown and armband to David. Most readers see him as an opportunist who stripped the body and invented the story, hoping for a reward from Saul’s rival.

f.g: Probably a royal headband or diadem rather than a large crown.

f.w: the bracelet that was on his arm
f.g: An armlet, a band worn on the upper arm as royal insignia.

chapters.n: Instead of celebrating, David and his men tear their clothes in grief. David had never wanted Saul’s death, even after years of being hunted by him.
They mourn and fast all day — not only for Saul and Jonathan, but for the whole nation and the army of the Lord that had been struck down.

f.g: Even = evening. Fasting until sunset was a common expression of mourning (compare 1 Samuel 31:13).

chapters.n: David asks again where the man is from. He calls himself the son of a “stranger” — a foreign resident living in Israel — which means he should have known Israel’s reverence for the anointed king.

f.g: Hebrew ger — a resident foreigner who lived among Israel and was expected to know its laws.

chapters.n: David is stunned: how could anyone dare to raise his hand against the man God had anointed? David himself had twice refused to kill Saul when he had the chance.
David orders the man executed. The bearer of “good news” finds that David will not reward anyone for violence against Saul’s house.

f.g: An idiom meaning to attack and kill him.

chapters.n: By his own words the Amalekite convicted himself. Whether his story was true or false, he claimed the deed, and David holds him responsible.

f.w: Thy blood be upon thy head
f.g: You are responsible for your own death; your guilt is your own.

f.w: thy mouth hath testified against thee

chapters.n: David now composes a lament — a poem of grief — for Saul and Jonathan. It is one of the most moving funeral songs in all of scripture.

f.g: A formal song of mourning sung over the dead.

chapters.n: The poem was taught to the people of Judah and preserved in an ancient collection called the book of Jasher, which is no longer extant. “The bow” may be the name of the song itself.

f.g: The words “the use of” are added by the translators; the Hebrew simply says “the Bow,” possibly the lament’s title, since Jonathan’s bow is honored in verse 22.
Jasher = “the upright one”; a lost book of Israelite poetry.

chapters.n: The lament opens with its refrain: Israel’s glory has been killed on the hills. “How are the mighty fallen” repeats three times, like a tolling bell.

f.g: Or “the glory” or “the gazelle” of Israel — a poetic title for Saul and Jonathan.
This refrain appears in verses 19, 25, and 27, framing the poem.

chapters.n: David does not want the Philistine cities to hear the news and gloat. Gath and Askelon were two of the five main Philistine cities.

f.g: A Philistine city, home of Goliath and of King Achish.
Ashkelon, a Philistine city on the Mediterranean coast.
A term for the Philistines, who did not share Israel’s covenant sign of circumcision.

chapters.n: In poetic grief David curses the mountains where Saul died: may no dew or rain fall there. Saul’s shield lies defiled, as if he had never been anointed king.

f.g: Fields whose harvest could provide offerings; David wishes the hills to be barren.
Warriors oiled leather shields to keep them supple; the phrase also echoes Saul’s anointing as king.

chapters.n: David honors the two men as warriors: Jonathan’s bow and Saul’s sword never came back from battle without striking the enemy.
David speaks generously of Saul, remembering the father and son as loved and united to the end. Jonathan had stayed loyal to his father even while loving David.

f.w: in their death they were not divided

chapters.n: He calls on Israel’s women to mourn Saul, who brought prosperity to the nation — the spoils of his victories became fine clothing and jewelry for them.

f.g: Fine red-dyed cloth, a costly luxury.

chapters.n: The refrain returns, now focusing on Jonathan, lying slain on the heights.

f.g: Here simply the hills or heights where the battle was fought.

chapters.n: David’s most personal words: Jonathan’s loyal, covenant love for him was extraordinary, deeper than any love he had known. Their friendship is one of scripture’s great examples of selfless devotion.

f.g: Passing = surpassing. David is describing a friendship of covenant loyalty that exceeded even marriage in faithfulness.

chapters.n: The poem ends with the refrain a final time. The “weapons of war” may be a poetic way of speaking of Saul and Jonathan themselves.

f.g: Likely a metaphor for the fallen warriors, Israel’s defenders.

chapters.n: Before making any move toward the throne, David asks the Lord for direction. God sends him to Hebron, an ancient city of Judah tied to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

f.g: A city in the hill country of Judah, about 20 miles south of Jerusalem, where the patriarchs were buried.

chapters.n: David moves to Hebron with his two wives. Both women connect him to the region of Judah, which would help his acceptance there.

f.g: From Jezreel, a town in Judah (not the northern Jezreel).

chapters.n: The loyal band of men who had followed David during his years as a fugitive settle with their families in the towns around Hebron.

f.w: his men that were with him

chapters.n: David’s own tribe of Judah publicly anoints him king. This is his second anointing; Samuel had anointed him privately years before. David also learns that the men of Jabesh-gilead risked their lives to bury Saul.

f.g: A town east of the Jordan that Saul had once rescued; its men repaid him by recovering his body.

chapters.n: David sends a blessing to Jabesh-gilead, praising their loyalty to Saul. His respect for Saul is sincere, and it also shows Saul’s supporters that he is not their enemy.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal, covenant love; faithful kindness that goes beyond duty.

chapters.n: He prays that God will show them the same loyal love and faithfulness, and he promises to repay their kindness himself.

f.g: A common Hebrew pairing (ḥesed and ’emet): steadfast love and faithfulness, qualities especially of God.
Requite = repay.

chapters.n: David gently invites them to take courage — Saul is gone, and Judah has a new king. It is a diplomatic hint that they might accept him too.

f.g: Take courage; be strong.

chapters.n: Abner, Saul’s cousin and army commander, has other plans. He takes Saul’s surviving son Ish-bosheth to Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, safely away from the Philistines.

f.g: “Man of shame.” He is called Esh-baal (“man of Baal,” meaning master) in 1 Chronicles 8:33; later scribes often replaced “baal” in names with “bosheth” (shame).

chapters.n: Abner makes Ish-bosheth king over the northern and eastern tribes. In practice, Abner holds the real power.

f.g: Probably the tribe of Asher (or the Asherites); not the Assyrians.

chapters.n: Ish-bosheth’s reign is brief and weak. The nation is now split: the north under Saul’s son, and Judah under David — a preview of the later division of the kingdom.

f.g: The length differs from David’s seven and a half years in Hebron; the extra years may cover the time before Abner established Ish-bosheth.

chapters.n: David reigns over Judah from Hebron for seven and a half years before becoming king of all Israel.
The two sides move toward a confrontation. Abner leads Ish-bosheth’s men to Gibeon, a city in Benjamin north of Jerusalem.

f.g: A Benjaminite city about six miles northwest of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Joab, David’s nephew and commander, meets them. The two armies sit facing each other across a large pool — a scene of tense standoff.

f.g: Zeruiah was David’s sister, so Joab and his brothers were David’s nephews.
Archaeologists have found a large rock-cut water shaft at Gibeon (el-Jib) that may be this pool.

chapters.n: Abner proposes a contest of champions. “Play” sounds harmless, but it means a deadly combat between chosen young warriors.

f.g: Here a grim euphemism for a combat by champions, perhaps meant to settle the conflict with fewer deaths.

chapters.n: Twelve men from each side step forward — twelve Benjaminites for Saul’s house and twelve of David’s men.
Each man grabs his opponent and stabs him, and all twenty-four fall together. The contest settles nothing, and the place is named for the tragedy.

f.g: Hebrew: “field of flints” or “field of blades” (sharp edges).

chapters.n: Because the champions’ contest ended in a draw, full battle erupts. David’s men win decisively over Abner’s forces.
Three brothers, sons of David’s sister Zeruiah, are in the battle. The youngest, Asahel, is famous for his speed.

f.g: A gazelle, known for swiftness.

chapters.n: Asahel chases Abner himself, determined and single-minded, hoping to kill the enemy commander.

f.w: turned not to the right hand nor to the left
f.g: He kept straight on his target without distraction.

chapters.n: Abner, glancing back, recognizes the young man chasing him.
Abner, a veteran warrior, urges Asahel to go after an easier opponent and take his armor as a prize instead. Asahel refuses.

f.g: Here the weapons and gear of a defeated soldier, taken as plunder.

chapters.n: Abner pleads again. He doesn’t want to kill Asahel, knowing it would start a blood feud with Joab, Asahel’s powerful brother.

f.w: how then should I hold up my face to Joab
f.g: How could I face Joab? Killing his brother would bring shame and vengeance.

chapters.n: When Asahel still won’t stop, Abner thrusts back with the butt end of his spear so hard it goes through him. Everyone who reaches the spot halts in shock.

f.g: The back end of the spear, often pointed so it could be stuck in the ground.
The belly or abdomen.

chapters.n: Joab and Abishai keep chasing Abner until sunset, reaching a hill in the wilderness near Gibeon.

f.g: A hill whose exact location is unknown.

chapters.n: The Benjaminites, Saul’s own tribe, regroup around Abner on a hilltop, ready to make a stand.
Abner calls for an end to the killing. Fighting fellow Israelites will only leave bitterness, he says — a wise plea, though it also saves his own troops.

f.w: Shall the sword devour for ever?
f.g: A vivid image of war as a beast that never stops eating.
A reminder that both sides are Israelites — this is civil war.

chapters.n: Joab swears by God that if Abner had not spoken, the chase would have gone on until morning. He agrees to stop.

f.g: A solemn oath: “as surely as God lives.”

chapters.n: Joab sounds the trumpet — the signal to halt — and the fighting ends for that day.

f.g: The shofar, a ram’s horn used to signal troops.

chapters.n: Abner’s men march all night, cross the Jordan, and return to their base at Mahanaim.

f.g: Possibly a ravine or region east of the Jordan; the meaning may be “the gorge.”

chapters.n: When Joab counts his men, David’s side has lost only nineteen soldiers — plus Asahel, whose death is singled out because it will shape later events.
Abner’s losses are far heavier: 360 men. The battle shows David’s growing strength.

f.g: Threescore = 60; so 360.

chapters.n: Asahel is buried in the family tomb in Bethlehem, David’s hometown. Joab marches through the night back to Hebron — carrying a grudge that will lead to Abner’s death in the next chapter.

f.g: A tomb, often cut into rock.

chapters.n: The civil war drags on, but the momentum is clearly with David. This one verse summarizes years of slow change: God’s chosen king rises while Saul’s dynasty fades.

f.g: Waxed = grew, became.

chapters.n: The narrator pauses to list David’s sons born in Hebron. Several of them — Amnon, Absalom, Adonijah — will become central, and tragic, figures later in the story.
Absalom’s mother was a princess of Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee. That royal connection will matter when Absalom later flees there.

f.g: Called Daniel in 1 Chronicles 3:1; he never appears again in the story.

chapters.n: Adonijah, the fourth son, will later try to seize the throne before Solomon.
Six sons by six different wives. Multiplying wives was a common royal practice for building alliances, but the law of Moses warned kings against it, and these rival households will bring heartache.

f.w: These were born to David in Hebron

chapters.n: Meanwhile, Abner is steadily strengthening his own position inside Saul’s house. He is the real power behind Ish-bosheth’s throne.
Ish-bosheth accuses Abner of sleeping with Saul’s concubine Rizpah. In that culture, taking a former king’s concubine could signal a claim to his throne, so this was a serious charge.

f.g: A secondary wife with lower legal status than a full wife.
A Hebrew idiom for sexual relations.

chapters.n: Abner explodes in anger. After all his loyalty to Saul’s family, does Ish-bosheth treat him like a worthless traitor over a woman?

f.g: An insult meaning “Am I a contemptible nobody?” Dogs were scavengers and despised in ancient Israel.
Wroth = very angry.

chapters.n: Abner swears a solemn oath that he will help bring about what God had promised David. It reveals that even Saul’s side knew of God’s promise.

f.w: So do God to Abner, and more also
f.g: A standard oath formula: “May God punish me severely if I don’t do this.”

f.w: as the LORD hath sworn to David

chapters.n: He vows to transfer the whole kingdom to David, from the far north to the far south.

f.g: Here translate = transfer.
A phrase meaning the entire land of Israel, from its northernmost to southernmost towns.

chapters.n: Ish-bosheth, completely dependent on Abner, is too afraid to say anything back. The scene shows how hollow his kingship is.
Abner opens secret negotiations with David, offering to bring all Israel over to him if David will make a covenant with him.

f.g: A rhetorical question, perhaps meaning “Who really controls the land?” — implying Abner does.
A covenant or treaty.

chapters.n: David agrees, but on one condition: Abner must bring back Michal, Saul’s daughter and David’s first wife. Restoring her would strengthen David’s legal tie to Saul’s house.
David also makes a formal request to Ish-bosheth, reminding him that he paid Saul a costly bride-price for Michal.

f.g: Espoused = betrothed, or formally married.

f.w: an hundred foreskins of the Philistines
f.g: Saul had asked for 100; David brought 200.

chapters.n: Ish-bosheth complies, taking Michal from the man Saul had given her to after David fled.

f.g: Also spelled Phalti.

chapters.n: A heartbreaking detail: her second husband follows her, weeping, until Abner orders him home. The politics of kings cause real human suffering.

f.g: A village near the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem, on the road toward Judah.

chapters.n: Abner lobbies the leaders of the northern tribes, reminding them that they had long wanted David as their king.

f.g: The senior men who led clans and tribes.

chapters.n: He cites a promise from the Lord that David would save Israel from the Philistines and other enemies — something Saul had failed to do.

f.w: By the hand of my servant David

chapters.n: Abner speaks especially to Benjamin, Saul’s own tribe, whose support mattered most. Then he travels to Hebron to report the agreements to David.

f.g: An idiom meaning to speak directly and personally to someone.

chapters.n: David receives Abner and twenty men with a feast — a traditional way of sealing a covenant of friendship.

f.w: made Abner and the men that were with him a feast

chapters.n: Abner promises to rally all Israel to make a covenant with David as king. David sends him away “in peace” — under his protection.

f.g: Repeated three times (verses 21-23), stressing that David had guaranteed Abner’s safety.

chapters.n: Just as Abner leaves, Joab returns from a raid with plunder. The timing sets up the tragedy.

f.g: A raiding band.

chapters.n: Joab is told that Abner — the man who killed his brother Asahel — has just been in Hebron and left peacefully.
Joab angrily confronts the king, scolding him for letting Abner go.

f.g: He has gotten clean away.

chapters.n: Joab claims Abner was really a spy. His true motives are likely revenge for Asahel and fear of losing his own place as commander to Abner.

f.w: thy going out and thy coming in
f.g: A Hebrew idiom for all of a person’s activities and movements.

chapters.n: Without David’s knowledge, Joab sends messengers to call Abner back.

f.g: A site a little north of Hebron.

chapters.n: Under the pretense of a private conversation at the city gate, Joab stabs Abner to death — in the same place Abner had struck Asahel. Hebron was a city of refuge, which makes the murder even more shocking.

f.g: Hebron was a city of refuge, where a manslayer was supposed to receive a fair hearing.

chapters.n: David publicly declares that he and his kingdom are innocent of Abner’s death. It was crucial that Israel not think David had arranged the killing.
David pronounces a curse on Joab’s family line: may it always suffer disease, weakness, violence, or poverty.

f.g: A bodily discharge; a chronic disease that made one ritually unclean (Leviticus 15).
Possibly a cripple, or, as some translate, one who works a spindle — doing “women’s work,” an insult in that culture.

chapters.n: The narrator explains the motive plainly: Joab and Abishai killed Abner to avenge Asahel. But Asahel died in battle, which made this personal revenge, not lawful justice.
David orders everyone, including Joab, to mourn publicly. The king himself walks behind the funeral bier, honoring Abner.

f.g: Coarse cloth, often of goat hair, worn as a sign of grief or repentance.
The frame on which a body was carried to burial.

chapters.n: Abner is buried in Hebron, and David weeps aloud at the grave. His grief is sincere and visible to all.
David composes a short lament asking whether Abner died like a “fool” — a reckless, senseless man.

f.g: Hebrew nabal — a morally foolish person (the same word as Nabal’s name in 1 Samuel 25).

chapters.n: Abner was no criminal in chains; he was a free man struck down by treachery. The people weep again.

f.g: Shackles for the feet.

chapters.n: David refuses to eat until sunset, fasting for Abner even when people urge him to eat.

f.g: In KJV English, “meat” means food in general.

chapters.n: The people notice and approve. David’s sincere conduct wins the trust of the nation.

f.w: whatsoever the king did pleased all the people

chapters.n: Everyone — Judah and the northern tribes alike — understands that the king had no part in Abner’s murder. This was essential for uniting the kingdom.
David honors Abner as a “prince and a great man” — a generous tribute to a former enemy.

f.g: A leader or commander, not necessarily a king’s son.

chapters.n: David admits his weakness: his violent nephews are too strong for him to control. He leaves their punishment to God; Solomon will later deal with Joab.

f.w: the sons of Zeruiah be too hard for me
the LORD shall reward the doer of evil

chapters.n: When Ish-bosheth hears that Abner is dead, he loses all courage, and the northern tribes are thrown into alarm. Without Abner, Saul’s house has no strong leader left.

f.g: An idiom for losing heart or courage.

chapters.n: Two of Ish-bosheth’s own officers are introduced — brothers from Beeroth, a town in Benjamin. They were from Saul’s tribe, making their coming betrayal even darker.

f.g: Leaders of raiding units.
Originally one of the Gibeonite towns, later counted as part of Benjamin.

chapters.n: A side note explains that the original people of Beeroth had fled to Gittaim and still lived there as foreigners when this account was written.

f.g: Sojourners = temporary residents, people living away from their homeland.
Until the time the narrator was writing.

chapters.n: The narrator introduces Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, who was crippled as a little boy when his nurse dropped him while fleeing after Saul’s death. He is the last real heir of Saul’s line, and he will reappear in chapter 9.

f.g: Called Merib-baal in 1 Chronicles 8:34; like Ish-bosheth, “bosheth” (shame) seems to replace “baal.”
The valley where Saul’s last battle took place.

chapters.n: The brothers come to Ish-bosheth’s house during the hottest part of the day, when he is taking his noonday rest.

f.g: In the Near East people often rested during the midday heat.

chapters.n: Pretending to collect wheat — perhaps as officers drawing supplies — they get inside and stab him.

f.g: In the belly; the same phrase used for the deaths of Asahel and Abner (2 Samuel 2:23; 3:27).

chapters.n: They kill Ish-bosheth in his bed, cut off his head, and travel all night through the Jordan valley toward Hebron.

f.g: Hebrew Arabah — the Jordan Rift Valley.

chapters.n: Expecting a reward, they present the head to David and claim God has avenged him on Saul’s family. They even try to speak in religious terms to justify murder.
David answers with a solemn oath, invoking the God who has rescued him from every danger. David did not need assassins; the Lord had always been his deliverer.

f.w: redeemed my soul out of all adversity

chapters.n: David reminds them of the Amalekite who claimed to have killed Saul and expected a reward — and was executed instead.
If that man deserved death, how much more do men who murdered an innocent man asleep in his own bed? David calls Ish-bosheth “righteous” — not guilty of any crime deserving death.

f.w: require his blood of your hand
f.g: Hold you accountable for his death.

chapters.n: The murderers are executed and their bodies publicly displayed as a warning. David gives Ish-bosheth’s head an honorable burial in Abner’s tomb, again showing respect for Saul’s house.
With Saul’s house gone, all the tribes come to David at Hebron. They declare they are his own family — fellow Israelites bound to him by blood.

f.w: we are thy bone and thy flesh
f.g: An idiom of close kinship.

chapters.n: They recall that David had led Israel’s armies even in Saul’s day, and that the Lord had called him to shepherd His people. The image of the king as shepherd points ahead to Christ, the Good Shepherd.

f.g: Led Israel’s army out to battle and back home again.

f.w: Thou shalt feed my people Israel
f.g: Feed = shepherd, tend.

chapters.n: The elders make a covenant with David before the Lord and anoint him king over all Israel. This is David’s third anointing: first privately by Samuel, then by Judah, now by the whole nation.
David began reigning at age thirty and ruled forty years in all.
His reign divides into two parts: about seven and a half years over Judah from Hebron, then thirty-three years over the united kingdom from Jerusalem.
David moves against Jerusalem, still held by the Canaanite Jebusites. Its defenders mock him, boasting that even blind and lame men could keep him out of their fortress.

f.g: A Canaanite people who had held Jerusalem since before Joshua’s time.

chapters.n: Despite the taunts, David captures the stronghold of Zion, which becomes known as the City of David. Zion will become a rich symbol in scripture for God’s holy city and people.

f.g: Originally the fortified hill of Jebusite Jerusalem; later a name for the temple mount, Jerusalem, and God’s covenant people.

chapters.n: David offers command to whoever climbs up the water shaft and conquers the city, turning the Jebusites’ taunt back on them. A saying grew from this event. In Chronicles, Joab is the one who succeeds.

f.g: Probably a water channel or shaft leading into the city from the Gihon spring.

f.w: he shall be chief and captain

chapters.n: David makes the fortress his home and expands the city, building outward from the Millo.

f.g: Probably “fill” — a terraced earthwork supporting buildings on the hillside.

chapters.n: David’s greatness grows, and the narrator gives the reason: the Lord was with him.

f.g: Hosts = armies; the Lord as commander of heavenly and earthly forces.

chapters.n: Hiram, the Phoenician king of Tyre, sends materials and skilled workers to build David a palace — the first sign of international respect for the new king.

f.g: Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician port city on the coast north of Israel, famous for its cedar trade.

chapters.n: David recognizes that his success comes from God, and that God exalted him not for his own glory but for the sake of Israel. Leadership is a stewardship for others.
David takes more wives and concubines in Jerusalem. The narrator reports this without comment, but the law warned kings not to multiply wives, and the consequences will follow.
The list of sons born in Jerusalem includes Nathan and Solomon. Solomon will become king, and the Gospel of Luke traces Jesus’ genealogy through Nathan.
More of David’s Jerusalem-born sons are listed.
The list concludes. These names show how large David’s royal household had become.

f.g: “God is deliverance.” Many of these names honor God (El).

chapters.n: The Philistines, who may have tolerated David as a rival to Saul, now see a united Israel under him as a threat and come to attack. David withdraws to a stronghold.

f.g: A fortress or stronghold, perhaps the one where David had hidden earlier.

chapters.n: The Philistines spread out in the valley of Rephaim, just southwest of Jerusalem.

f.g: A broad valley near Jerusalem; Rephaim was also the name of an ancient race of giants.

chapters.n: As always, David asks the Lord before going to battle, and the Lord promises victory.
David wins, crediting the Lord for bursting through the enemy like a flood breaking through a dam. He names the place to commemorate it.

f.g: “Lord of breakings through.” Here “baal” simply means lord or master.

chapters.n: The fleeing Philistines leave their idols behind, and David’s men burn them, as the law commanded.
The Philistines return and take up the same position in the valley.
This time the Lord gives different instructions: do not attack head-on, but circle around behind them. God’s guidance is not a formula; David must ask each time.

f.g: Go around; make a circling maneuver.
The exact tree is uncertain; possibly balsam or baca trees.

chapters.n: The signal to attack will be the sound of marching in the treetops — the Lord’s own army going ahead of David.

f.g: The sound of marching footsteps.
Act quickly; spring into action.

chapters.n: David obeys exactly, and he drives the Philistines from Geba all the way to Gezer, near their own territory. His obedience brings complete victory.

f.g: Gezer, a city on the western edge of the hill country, toward Philistine lands.

chapters.n: Now secure as king, David turns to a spiritual goal: bringing the ark of the covenant to his new capital. He gathers a huge honor guard of chosen men.

The ark had sat neglected for about two decades at Baale (Kirjath-jearim). It was Israel’s most sacred object, the symbol of God’s presence, called by His name and pictured as His throne between the cherubim.

f.g: Another name for Kirjath-jearim, about nine miles west of Jerusalem.
The two golden cherubim on the ark’s lid (the mercy seat) were seen as the footstool or throne of the invisible God.

chapters.n: They put the ark on a brand-new ox cart. It looked honorable, but the law said the ark must be carried on poles on the shoulders of Levites. The Philistines had once moved it by cart, and Israel copies them.

f.g: Here simply “the hill” — the hill in Kirjath-jearim where Abinadab lived.

chapters.n: Abinadab’s son Ahio walks in front of the ark, guiding the oxen, while his brother Uzzah walks beside it.
A grand procession follows, with joyful music on every kind of instrument. Their intentions are good and their worship is sincere.

f.g: Celebrated with music and dancing.
Chronicles reads “with all their might and with singing” (1 Chronicles 13:8); the Hebrew words are similar.
Psalteries = stringed instruments like lyres or harps; timbrels = hand drums or tambourines.

chapters.n: At a threshing floor the oxen stumble, and Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark.

f.g: A flat, hard open area where grain was beaten to separate it from the husks.

chapters.n: God strikes Uzzah dead. It seems severe to modern readers, but the law warned that even Levites must not touch the holy things. The lesson: sacred things must be handled in God’s way, not merely with good intentions.

f.w: God smote him there for his error

f.g: The Hebrew word is uncertain; it may mean rashness or irreverence.

chapters.n: David is upset and names the place “the breaking out against Uzzah.” The joyful event has turned to tragedy.

f.g: “The breach (or outburst) against Uzzah.” Compare Baal-perazim in 2 Samuel 5:20.

chapters.n: David is afraid. He realizes that God’s holy presence is not something to take lightly, and wonders whether he can bring the ark near at all.

f.w: How shall the ark of the LORD come to me?

chapters.n: So he leaves it at the house of Obed-edom, a man from Gath — perhaps a Philistine follower of David, or a Levite from the town of Gath-rimmon.

f.g: Gittite = from Gath. A Levite named Obed-edom later serves the ark (1 Chronicles 15:18, 24).

chapters.n: For three months the ark stays there, and the Lord blesses Obed-edom’s whole household. God’s presence, treated with reverence, brings blessing rather than judgment.
Encouraged by the blessings on Obed-edom’s house, David tries again, this time with great joy. Chronicles adds that now the Levites carried the ark properly.
After the bearers take just six steps — and nothing goes wrong — David offers sacrifices, thanking God and seeking His acceptance.

f.g: Fattened animals, choice offerings.

chapters.n: David dances with all his strength in pure joy before the Lord. He wears a simple linen ephod, a priestly-style garment, instead of his royal robes.

f.w: danced before the LORD with all his might

f.g: A short linen garment worn by priests and those serving in worship.

chapters.n: The whole nation joins in with shouts and trumpet blasts, bringing the ark up to Jerusalem.

f.g: The shofar, a ram’s-horn trumpet.

chapters.n: Michal, Saul’s daughter, watches from a window and despises David in her heart. Note that she is called “Saul’s daughter” here, not David’s wife — the narrator hints at where her loyalties lie.
The ark is placed in a tent David had set up for it. He offers burnt offerings (fully devoted to God) and peace offerings (shared in a fellowship meal).
Like a father of the nation, David blesses the people in the Lord’s name.
David gives every person, women and men alike, a gift of food to celebrate. The whole nation shares in the joy.

f.g: The Hebrew probably means a cake of raisins or dates rather than a jug of wine.

chapters.n: Michal meets David with biting sarcasm, accusing him of shamelessly exposing himself before servant girls, acting undignified for a king.

f.g: Without his royal robe, the short ephod may have exposed more than was considered proper for a king.
Empty, worthless men.

chapters.n: David replies that he was worshipping the Lord, who chose him over Saul’s family. His joy was directed to God, not to impressing people.

f.w: which chose me before thy father

chapters.n: David says he will humble himself even more before God, and the humble servant girls will honor him for it. True greatness comes through humility before the Lord.

f.g: Base = lowly, humble.

f.w: of them shall I be had in honour

chapters.n: Michal remains childless all her life. Whatever the cause, this means no descendant of Saul would sit on David’s throne.

f.g: Childlessness was a deep sorrow in Israel; here it also marks the end of Saul’s hopes through Michal.

chapters.n: This is one of the most important chapters in the Old Testament. David is settled in his palace, and for a time the Lord has given him peace from his enemies.

f.w: rest round about from all his enemies

chapters.n: David tells the prophet Nathan he feels uneasy living in a cedar palace while the ark of God sits in a tent. He wants to build God a temple.

f.g: In a tent, like the tabernacle of Moses’ day.

chapters.n: Nathan, sensing David’s good heart, encourages him at once. But he answers before asking the Lord — even a prophet speaks from his own judgment at times.

f.w: Go, do all that is in thine heart

chapters.n: That very night the Lord speaks to Nathan with a different message.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto Nathan

chapters.n: The Lord asks David a question that sets up a beautiful wordplay: “Will you build Me a house?” The answer will be that God will build David a house instead.

f.g: “House” means three things in this chapter: a palace, a temple, and a dynasty (royal family line).

chapters.n: God reminds David that He has always traveled with His people, living in a tent since the Exodus. He has never needed a permanent building.

f.w: walked in a tent and in a tabernacle

chapters.n: In all that time, God never asked any of Israel’s leaders for a cedar temple. The initiative for blessing comes from God, not from human gifts to Him.

f.g: 1 Chronicles 17:6 reads “judges,” which fits the context of leaders who shepherded Israel.

chapters.n: God recalls David’s humble beginning: He took him from tending sheep to rule over His people.

f.g: A sheep pen or pasture.

f.w: I took thee from the sheepcote

chapters.n: The Lord has been with David everywhere, removed his enemies, and made his name great — an echo of God’s promise to Abraham.
God promises a secure homeland where Israel will be planted and no longer harassed by wicked enemies, as they had been in the days of the judges.
Then comes the great reversal: David wanted to build God a house, but the Lord will build David a “house” — a lasting royal dynasty.

f.w: he will make thee an house

chapters.n: After David dies, God will raise up one of his own sons and establish his kingdom.

f.g: A gentle idiom for dying and being buried with one’s ancestors.

chapters.n: That son — Solomon — will build the temple. And God will establish his throne “for ever,” a promise ultimately fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the Son of David.

f.w: He shall build an house for my name

chapters.n: God will relate to David’s son as a father to a son, disciplining him when he sins. Hebrews applies “I will be his father” to Christ, the perfect Son who never needed correction.

f.w: I will be his father, and he shall be my son

f.g: Ordinary human discipline — punishment through people and events.

chapters.n: Unlike Saul, David’s line will not lose God’s covenant mercy, even when individual kings fail.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — God’s loyal, covenant love.

f.w: as I took it from Saul

chapters.n: David’s house, kingdom, and throne will be established forever. Later prophets looked to this promise in hoping for the Messiah; Latter-day Saints see its fulfillment in Christ, the eternal King.

f.w: thy throne shall be established for ever

chapters.n: Nathan faithfully delivers everything the Lord revealed, even though it corrects his own earlier advice.

f.g: A revelation received by a prophet; here a revelation in the night.

chapters.n: Overwhelmed, David goes in and sits before the Lord — probably in the tent where the ark was kept — and begins a prayer of humble wonder: “Who am I?”

f.w: Who am I, O Lord GOD?

f.g: When “GOD” is in capitals after “Lord,” the Hebrew is Adonai YHWH — “Lord Jehovah.” Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah as the premortal Jesus Christ.

chapters.n: Already God had done much, but now He has promised blessings for David’s descendants far into the future. David marvels at this kind of generous treatment.

f.w: is this the manner of man
f.g: A difficult phrase; possibly “Is this how you deal with mere men?” or “This is instruction for mankind.”

chapters.n: David is at a loss for words — God already knows him completely.

f.w: thou, Lord GOD, knowest thy servant

chapters.n: God did all this because of His own word and His own heart — out of grace, not because David earned it.
David praises God’s greatness: there is no one like Him, and no other God.
David also praises Israel’s unique story: God personally redeemed them from Egypt to be His own people.

f.g: Awe-inspiring, fearsome — not “bad.”

chapters.n: God has made Israel His covenant people forever, and He has become their God.

f.w: a people unto thee for ever

chapters.n: David asks God to do exactly what He has promised. Good prayer often takes God’s own words and asks Him to fulfill them.
David’s deepest wish is that God’s name be honored forever, and that his own family remain faithful before Him.
Because God revealed this promise, David found the courage to pray this way. Revelation gives confidence in prayer.

f.g: Found the courage or boldness.

chapters.n: David affirms that God is the true God and that His words can be trusted completely.
He closes by asking God to bless his house forever. This covenant with David becomes a foundation of Israel’s hope for a coming Messiah from David’s line.

f.w: with thy blessing let the house of thy servant be blessed for ever

chapters.n: This chapter summarizes David’s military victories, which fulfilled God’s promise to give Israel rest. First, David subdues the Philistines, Israel’s longtime oppressors.

f.g: Possibly “the bridle of the mother city” — control of the Philistines’ chief city. 1 Chronicles 18:1 says “Gath and her towns.”

chapters.n: David conquers Moab and executes two-thirds of its captured soldiers, measured by lines as they lay on the ground. It is a harsh practice of ancient warfare, recorded plainly. Moab becomes a tributary state.

f.g: David’s great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite, and he had once sheltered his parents there (1 Samuel 22:3-4), which makes this conflict striking.
Paid tribute — regular payments from a conquered nation.

chapters.n: David defeats Hadadezer, king of Zobah, a powerful Aramean (Syrian) kingdom north of Damascus, as Israel’s influence stretches toward the Euphrates.

f.g: God had promised Abraham’s descendants land as far as the Euphrates.

chapters.n: David captures a large force and disables most of the chariot horses, keeping only enough for a hundred chariots. Israel was not to trust in horses and chariots for its strength.

f.g: Hamstrung — cut the leg tendons so the horses could not be used in war.

chapters.n: When the Arameans of Damascus come to help Hadadezer, David defeats them too.

f.g: Succour = help, aid.
The leading city of Aram (Syria), northeast of Israel.

chapters.n: David stations garrisons in Damascus, and Syria pays him tribute. The narrator stresses the key point: the Lord gave David victory wherever he went.

f.w: the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went

chapters.n: David brings the gold shields of Hadadezer’s officers back to Jerusalem as trophies.
He also takes a great deal of bronze from Hadadezer’s cities. Chronicles says Solomon later used this bronze to make temple furnishings.

f.g: In the KJV, “brass” usually means bronze, an alloy of copper and tin.

chapters.n: Toi, king of Hamath in Syria, hears of David’s victory over Hadadezer, his own enemy.

f.g: A city-state on the Orontes River in Syria, north of Zobah.

chapters.n: Toi sends his son with rich gifts to congratulate David and seek his friendship.

f.g: To greet him; to offer formal congratulations.

chapters.n: Instead of keeping the treasure for himself, David dedicates it to the Lord — a store that would help build the future temple.
The list of nations shows how broadly David’s kingdom now reached, and that all its plunder was devoted to God.
David wins fame by defeating a large army in the Valley of Salt, south of the Dead Sea. Many manuscripts and 1 Chronicles read “Edomites” here instead of “Syrians,” which fits verse 14.

f.g: A valley near the Dead Sea, probably in the region of Edom.
In Hebrew, “Aram” (Syria) and “Edom” look very similar and were easily confused by copyists.

chapters.n: Edom also comes under David’s control. The refrain repeats that the Lord preserved David everywhere he went.

f.g: Descendants of Esau, Jacob’s twin; this fulfilled the prophecy that the elder would serve the younger.

chapters.n: Beyond conquest, David rules with justice and fairness for all his people — the true mark of a godly king.

f.g: Judgment = fair decisions; together the words mean doing what is right.

chapters.n: A list of David’s chief officials begins. Joab commands the army, and Jehoshaphat is the “recorder,” likely the royal herald or chief of state records.

f.g: Possibly the official who kept records and announced the king’s decisions.

chapters.n: Zadok and Ahimelech serve as priests, and Seraiah as royal secretary. Elsewhere Abiathar is the son of Ahimelech, so the names may have been reversed by a copyist.

f.g: A royal secretary who handled official documents and correspondence.

chapters.n: Benaiah commands David’s foreign bodyguard. David’s sons are called “chief rulers”; the Hebrew word usually means priests, perhaps meaning royal advisers or officials.

f.g: Probably Cretans and Philistines who served as David’s loyal royal guard.
Hebrew kohanim, normally “priests”; 1 Chronicles 18:17 says “chief about the king.”

chapters.n: Now secure, David remembers his covenant with Jonathan and asks whether anyone from Saul’s family is still alive so he can show them kindness. Ancient kings often wiped out rival families; David does the opposite.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — loyal, covenant love.

chapters.n: Ziba, a former servant of Saul’s household, is summoned to give information.
David speaks of showing “the kindness of God” — the generous, faithful love God shows. Ziba mentions Jonathan’s son, who is disabled in both feet.

f.g: Kindness like God’s own: undeserved, loyal, and generous.

chapters.n: Mephibosheth is living in Lo-debar, east of the Jordan, in the home of Machir — a man who later helps David too.

f.g: The name may mean “no pasture” or “nothing” — a fitting picture of his humble, hidden life.

chapters.n: David sends for him. For Saul’s grandson, a summons from the new king could have felt terrifying.
Mephibosheth falls on his face before David in fear and submission, calling himself the king’s servant.

f.g: Bowed low to show respect and submission.

chapters.n: David’s first words are “Fear not.” He restores Saul’s family land to him and invites him to eat at the royal table for the rest of his life — an honor usually reserved for the king’s own family.

f.w: eat bread at my table continually

chapters.n: Mephibosheth is overwhelmed and calls himself a “dead dog,” the lowest possible term. His humility mirrors how unworthy anyone feels before undeserved grace.

f.g: A phrase of extreme self-abasement — something worthless and contemptible.

chapters.n: David formally transfers all of Saul’s estates to Mephibosheth before Ziba as a witness.
Ziba and his large household will farm the land and supply its produce, but Mephibosheth himself will always eat with the king.

f.g: Till = farm, cultivate.
A large household, showing Ziba was a man of some wealth and influence.

chapters.n: Ziba promises to obey. David repeats that Mephibosheth will eat at his table “as one of the king’s sons.” Many readers see in this a picture of grace: the Lord welcomes the broken into His family because of a covenant made with another.

f.w: as one of the king's sons

chapters.n: Mephibosheth has a young son, Micha, so Jonathan’s line continues. Ziba’s whole household now serves him.
The chapter ends with a tender image: the disabled son of Jonathan living in Jerusalem, a permanent guest at the king’s table. His lameness is mentioned again to highlight how freely he was honored.
The king of Ammon, a nation east of the Jordan, dies, and his son Hanun takes the throne. This war sets the stage for the story of David and Bath-sheba.

f.g: The Ammonites, descendants of Lot, lived around Rabbah (modern Amman, Jordan).

chapters.n: David sends a delegation to express condolences, remembering some kindness Nahash had shown him — perhaps during his years as a fugitive from Saul.

f.g: Nahash had fought Saul, so he may have favored David as Saul’s rival.
Show ḥesed, loyal friendship, as between allies.

chapters.n: Hanun’s advisers convince him that David’s messengers are really spies plotting to take the city.

f.g: Leading officials or nobles.

chapters.n: Hanun publicly humiliates the envoys — shaving half their beards and cutting their robes to expose them. In that culture this was a deep insult to David himself.

f.w: shaved off the one half of their beards
f.g: A full beard was a sign of dignity and manhood; shaving it was a grave disgrace.

chapters.n: David sends word to spare them further shame: they can stay at Jericho until their beards grow back. He protects the dignity of his servants.

f.g: Tarry = stay, wait.
A town near the Jordan crossing, the first stop inside Israel on their way home.

chapters.n: Realizing they have made David their enemy, the Ammonites hire a large army of Aramean (Syrian) mercenaries.

f.g: An idiom: they had become offensive, hated by David.
Maacah was a small Aramean kingdom; the text means “the king of Maacah.”

chapters.n: David sends Joab with the army’s best warriors.
The Ammonites line up at their city gate, while the Syrian forces wait in the open field — trapping Israel between two armies.

f.g: Arranged their troops in battle formation.

chapters.n: Joab, seeing enemies in front and behind, takes the best troops to face the Syrians himself.
He gives the rest of the army to his brother Abishai to face the Ammonites.
The brothers agree to come to each other’s aid if either side starts to lose — a plan of mutual support.

Joab’s battle cry is one of the finest moments in his career: be courageous for our people and God’s cities, and leave the outcome to the Lord. It is a model of doing one’s best and trusting God with the result.

f.g: Act like men; show courage.

f.w: the LORD do that which seemeth him good

chapters.n: Joab advances on the Syrians, and they flee.
Seeing their hired allies run, the Ammonites retreat into their city. Joab returns to Jerusalem without besieging it, perhaps because the season was ending.

f.g: The city was Rabbah, the Ammonite capital.

chapters.n: The defeated Syrians regroup for a larger campaign.
Hadarezer calls in Aramean forces from beyond the Euphrates, led by his commander Shobach, and they gather at Helam.

f.g: The same king as Hadadezer in chapter 8; the spelling varies.
East of the Euphrates.
A place east of the Jordan, probably in northern Gilead.

chapters.n: This time David himself leads all Israel across the Jordan to fight them.
David wins a crushing victory and kills Shobach, the enemy commander. (1 Chronicles 19:18 gives slightly different numbers.)
The Aramean vassal kings make peace with Israel and become subject to it. The Ammonites are left to face David alone — as the next chapter will show.
In spring, the usual season for military campaigns, David sends his army to besiege Rabbah, the Ammonite capital. But David himself stays home — the first hint that he is not where he should be.

f.w: the time when kings go forth to battle
f.g: Spring, after the winter rains and before harvest, when roads were passable.
The Ammonite capital, modern Amman, Jordan.

chapters.n: Rising from an afternoon rest, David walks on his palace roof and sees a beautiful woman bathing. The temptation begins with idleness and a lingering look.

f.g: Late afternoon or evening.
Flat roofs were common living spaces; the palace stood above the houses of the city.

chapters.n: David inquires and learns she is Bath-sheba, wife of Uriah — one of his own elite soldiers. Knowing she is married should have stopped him.

f.g: “Daughter of an oath” or “daughter of abundance.”
Possibly the son of Ahithophel, David’s counselor, which may explain Ahithophel’s later betrayal.
A foreigner by ancestry but a faithful worshipper of Jehovah; his name means “the LORD is my light.”

chapters.n: David sends for her and sleeps with her. As king, he holds all the power in this encounter. The note that she had just completed ritual purification shows the child could only be David’s.

f.g: The verb shows David’s initiative and royal power.
She had finished the purification after her monthly period, so she was not already pregnant by Uriah.

chapters.n: Bath-sheba sends David three words in Hebrew: “I am pregnant.” David now faces a choice between confession and cover-up.
David chooses the cover-up, calling Uriah home from the battlefield.
David pretends interest in the war, asking how Joab, the troops, and the fighting are doing.

f.g: Literally “the peace (shalom) of Joab” — a bitterly ironic phrase given what follows.

chapters.n: David urges Uriah to go home and relax, sending him a gift of food. He hopes Uriah will sleep with his wife so the child will seem to be his.

f.g: Relax at home; possibly a hint at marital relations.
A portion of food; a gift from the king’s table.

chapters.n: But Uriah sleeps at the palace entrance with the guards and never goes home.
Puzzled, David asks why he didn’t go home after his long journey.
Uriah’s answer is noble and painful: the ark and his fellow soldiers are in tents in the field — how could he enjoy his home and wife? This foreign-born soldier shows more integrity than the king.

f.g: The ark sometimes went with the army into battle.
Soldiers on campaign often kept themselves from sexual relations (1 Samuel 21:5).

chapters.n: David asks him to stay one more day, still scheming.
David gets Uriah drunk, hoping to weaken his resolve. Even drunk, Uriah is more faithful than David sober — he still does not go home.
Out of options, David writes a letter to Joab and has Uriah carry it — unknowingly delivering his own death sentence.
David orders Joab to put Uriah where the fighting is fiercest and then pull back, leaving him to be killed. Adultery has led to murder.

f.g: Retire = withdraw, pull back.

f.w: that he may be smitten, and die

chapters.n: Joab carries out the order, placing Uriah where he knows the strongest defenders are.

f.g: The strongest, most skilled enemy fighters.

chapters.n: The Ammonites sally out, and several of David’s soldiers are killed, including Uriah. David’s sin costs other innocent lives as well.
Joab sends a messenger with a full report of the battle.
He carefully coaches the messenger on what to say.
Joab expects David may be angry that they went so close to the city wall, a well-known military blunder.
Joab anticipates David citing the story of Abimelech, killed by a woman who dropped a millstone from a wall. The messenger is to answer with one sentence that will calm the king: Uriah is dead too.

f.g: Jerubbesheth = Jerubbaal, Gideon’s other name, with “baal” replaced by “besheth” (shame).
A town in the hill country of Ephraim.

chapters.n: The messenger delivers the report as instructed.
He explains that the enemy came out against them, and Israel drove them back to the city gate.

f.g: Gained the advantage over us at first.

chapters.n: Archers on the wall killed some of the king’s men — and Uriah is dead too. The messenger mentions it right away, perhaps to avoid David’s anger.

f.g: Archers.

chapters.n: David responds with a cold proverb about the randomness of war, telling Joab not to be troubled. The man who once mourned Saul and Abner now shrugs off a murder he arranged.

f.w: the sword devoureth one as well as another
f.g: In war, anyone may die — David uses this to hide his guilt.

chapters.n: Bath-sheba mourns her husband, probably for the customary period.

f.g: Mourning usually lasted about seven days (Genesis 50:10; 1 Samuel 31:13).

chapters.n: David marries her, and a son is born. Outwardly the cover-up has worked — but the final line turns everything: what David did was evil in the Lord’s eyes. Nothing is hidden from God.

f.g: Literally “was evil in the eyes of the LORD.”

f.w: the thing that David had done

chapters.n: The Lord sends the prophet Nathan to confront David. Wisely, Nathan doesn’t accuse him directly but tells a story, as if presenting a legal case for the king to judge.

f.g: The parable lets David judge the situation honestly before realizing it is about himself.

chapters.n: The rich man has huge flocks and herds — more than he could ever need.
The poor man has just one little lamb that he loves like a daughter. The tender details — eating from his plate, sleeping in his arms — make the injustice deeply personal.

f.g: A female lamb.
Slept in his arms — a picture of love and closeness, echoing how a wife is cherished.

chapters.n: When a guest arrives, the rich man refuses to use his own animals and instead takes and cooks the poor man’s only lamb.

f.g: Dress = prepare for a meal.

chapters.n: David is furious and swears the man deserves to die. Without realizing it, he has pronounced judgment on himself.

f.g: Literally “is a son of death” — deserves death.

chapters.n: David also rules that the man must repay four lambs, as the law required. Tradition notes that four of David’s sons later suffered or died.
Nathan’s four Hebrew words cut to the heart: “You are the man.” Then he speaks for the Lord, recounting all God had done for David.

f.g: In Hebrew just two words: ’attah ha’ish.

chapters.n: God had given David everything — Saul’s kingdom and household, all Israel and Judah — and would have given more if he had asked.

f.g: The harem of a former king passed to his successor as a sign of royal authority.

chapters.n: God names the sins plainly: David despised the Lord’s commandment, murdered Uriah using the enemy’s sword, and took his wife.

f.w: despised the commandment of the LORD

chapters.n: The consequence: violence will never leave David’s household. In the coming chapters three of his sons — Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah — die violently.

f.w: the sword shall never depart from thine house

chapters.n: Trouble will rise from within David’s own family, and his wives will be taken publicly by another — fulfilled when Absalom rebels.

f.w: lie with thy wives in the sight of this sun

chapters.n: David sinned in secret, but his punishment will be public. What is done in darkness is brought into the light.

David doesn’t make excuses; he confesses simply, “I have sinned against the Lord.” Nathan says David will not die, as the law required for adultery and murder. Latter-day Saint scripture teaches that David’s sin against Uriah still cost him eternal blessings.

f.w: I have sinned against the LORD

chapters.n: Because David’s sin gave God’s enemies a reason to mock the Lord and His people, the child will die. Our sins can harm the reputation of God’s work.

f.w: given great occasion to the enemies of the LORD to blaspheme

chapters.n: Nathan leaves, and the baby becomes seriously ill. Note that the child’s mother is called “Uriah’s wife,” a reminder of the wrong done.
David pleads with God for the child, fasting and lying on the ground all night in sackcloth-like humility.

f.g: Besought = earnestly begged.

chapters.n: His senior servants try to lift him up and get him to eat, but he refuses.
On the seventh day the child dies. The servants are afraid to tell David, fearing what he might do in his grief.

f.g: Do himself harm; be overwhelmed with distress.

chapters.n: David notices them whispering and realizes the child is gone.
To everyone’s surprise, David gets up, washes, changes clothes, worships at the Lord’s house, and then eats. He accepts God’s will and turns to Him in worship even in sorrow.

f.g: Put on oil — a sign of ending mourning (compare 2 Samuel 14:2).
The tent sanctuary where the ark was kept; the temple was not yet built.

chapters.n: His servants are confused: he mourned while the child lived, but stopped once it died.
David explains that while the child lived, there was hope that God might be gracious.
Now nothing can bring the child back — but David expresses hope that he will go to his son one day. Latter-day Saints teach that little children who die are saved through Christ’s Atonement.

f.w: I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me

chapters.n: David comforts Bath-sheba, and she bears another son, Solomon. The narrator adds a tender note of grace: the Lord loved him.

f.g: Related to shalom — “peace” or “his replacement.”

chapters.n: Through Nathan, the Lord gives the baby a second name, Jedidiah, “beloved of the LORD.” The same prophet who brought judgment now brings a sign of God’s continuing favor.

f.g: “Beloved of Jehovah”; it shares a root with David’s name, which also suggests “beloved.”

chapters.n: The story returns to the war that framed David’s sin. Joab captures the part of Rabbah that holds the royal quarter.

f.g: Perhaps the citadel or the part of the city containing the palace.

chapters.n: Joab reports that he has taken the “city of waters” — the city’s water supply — so the rest of the city cannot hold out long.

f.g: Likely the lower city or fortification protecting the water source.

chapters.n: Joab urges David to come and finish the conquest himself, so the victory will be credited to the king — perhaps a pointed reminder that David belongs with his army.
David finally goes to battle and takes Rabbah.
David takes the crown of the Ammonite king (or of their god Milcom), a massive gold crown weighing about a talent, and much plunder.

f.g: The Hebrew malkam can mean “their king” or Milcom, the Ammonite god (1 Kings 11:5).
A talent weighed roughly 75 pounds (34 kg) — too heavy to wear long, so perhaps worn only briefly or on ceremonial occasions.

chapters.n: The Ammonite people are put to work with saws, picks, and axes and in brickmaking. Many translators read this as forced labor rather than torture. Then David and the army return to Jerusalem.

f.g: The Hebrew can mean he set them to work with saws — forced labor.
Possibly the brick mold — making bricks as forced labor.

chapters.n: Nathan’s warning that trouble would rise from David’s own house begins to come true. Amnon, David’s eldest son, becomes obsessed with his half-sister Tamar, the full sister of Absalom.

f.g: “Palm tree.” She and Absalom were children of Maacah (2 Samuel 3:3); Amnon was born to Ahinoam.
As the story shows, this was lust, not true love.

chapters.n: Amnon’s desire makes him sick with frustration. As an unmarried princess, Tamar was closely protected, so he saw no way to get to her.

f.g: Vexed = distressed, tormented.

chapters.n: Amnon’s cousin Jonadab, a clever and scheming man, enters the story.

f.g: Subtil = shrewd, crafty — the same quality used of the serpent in Genesis 3:1.
Also called Shammah, one of David’s older brothers.

chapters.n: Jonadab notices Amnon looking haggard and asks why. Amnon admits his desire for Tamar.

f.g: Thin, run-down, looking ill.

chapters.n: Jonadab devises a plan: pretend to be sick and ask the king to send Tamar to prepare food for him. It uses David’s care for his children against him.

f.g: Food in general.

chapters.n: Amnon follows the plan exactly and asks David for Tamar to bake him special cakes.

f.g: Possibly heart-shaped cakes or dumplings; the Hebrew word sounds like the word for “heart.”

chapters.n: David, unsuspecting, sends Tamar to help her brother. The king who once sent for Bath-sheba now unknowingly sends his daughter into danger.

f.g: Prepare food for him.

chapters.n: Tamar obediently goes and prepares the food in Amnon’s presence, as requested.
Amnon refuses to eat and orders everyone else to leave the room, isolating Tamar.

f.w: Have out all men from me
f.g: Send everyone out.

chapters.n: He asks Tamar to bring the food into his inner room so he can eat from her hand.
When she comes close, he grabs her and demands she sleep with him.
Tamar resists with dignity and clear moral reasoning: this is forbidden in Israel and would be a disgraceful, senseless act.

f.g: Do not humiliate or violate me.

f.w: no such thing ought to be done in Israel

f.g: Hebrew nebalah — a shameful outrage, a serious moral crime.

chapters.n: Tamar pleads: she would carry lifelong shame, and he would be counted among Israel’s worst fools. She even suggests asking the king for marriage — likely trying anything to escape.

f.w: he will not withhold me from thee
f.g: Though the law forbade such a marriage, Tamar may simply be desperate to buy time.

chapters.n: Amnon refuses to listen and, being stronger, rapes her. The narrator states it plainly, with no attempt to excuse it. The blame lies entirely with Amnon.
Immediately his “love” turns to intense hatred, revealing it was only selfish lust. He orders her out.

f.w: the hatred wherewith he hated her
f.g: Lust that uses another person often turns to contempt once satisfied.

chapters.n: Tamar protests that throwing her out is an even greater wrong, since it leaves her disgraced and abandoned without any protection. He still won’t listen.

f.g: Possibly “No!” or “There is no reason for this.”

chapters.n: Amnon calls a servant to throw “this woman” out and lock the door — he no longer even uses her name.

f.g: In Hebrew simply “this one” — a dehumanizing term.

chapters.n: Tamar wears the special robe of a royal virgin daughter. The servant puts her out and bolts the door.

f.g: Divers = various. Perhaps a long robe with sleeves, worn by the king’s unmarried daughters — the same rare phrase as Joseph’s coat.

chapters.n: Tamar shows her anguish publicly: ashes on her head, her royal robe torn, her hand on her head, crying aloud. She refuses to hide what was done to her.

f.g: A sign of deep mourning and grief.

f.w: laid her hand on her head
f.g: A gesture of grief or shame.

chapters.n: Absalom guesses what happened and tells Tamar to keep quiet for now. She lives the rest of her life desolate in his house — a deep injustice that no one in authority remedies.

f.g: Be quiet; don’t speak of it.
Alone, ruined, without marriage or future.

chapters.n: David is very angry, but he does nothing. The Greek Septuagint adds that he would not punish Amnon because he loved him as his firstborn. David’s failure to act sets up the next tragedy.

f.g: Wroth = angry. David’s own sin may have weakened his moral authority to discipline his sons.

chapters.n: Absalom says nothing at all to Amnon, but he hates him and quietly plans revenge.

f.g: An idiom for nothing at all.

chapters.n: Two years later, Absalom holds a sheep-shearing festival — a time of feasting — and invites all the king’s sons.

f.g: Sheep-shearing was a festive occasion with food and drink (1 Samuel 25:2-8).
A place about 15 miles north of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Absalom invites the king himself and his officials, perhaps knowing he would decline.
David declines so as not to be a burden, but gives Absalom his blessing.

f.g: A financial burden.

chapters.n: Absalom then asks that Amnon, the crown prince, come in David’s place. David seems uneasy.

f.w: Why should he go with thee?
f.g: David may sense something is wrong.

chapters.n: Absalom presses until David agrees to send Amnon and all his sons.

f.g: Urged him insistently.

chapters.n: Absalom orders his servants to kill Amnon when he is drunk, assuring them they act under his authority.
Absalom’s servants murder Amnon at the feast. The other princes flee in terror on their mules.

f.g: Mules were ridden by royalty in David’s time.

chapters.n: A false report reaches David first: all his sons have been killed.
David tears his clothes and lies on the ground in grief, and his servants do the same.

f.g: Tare = tore.

chapters.n: Jonadab — who had helped Amnon plan the crime — now coolly tells David that only Amnon is dead, revenge Absalom had planned since Tamar’s rape. Jonadab seems to know far too much.

f.g: By Absalom’s order or determination.

chapters.n: Jonadab reassures the king that he need not grieve as though all his sons were dead.
Absalom flees. A watchman sees a crowd coming down the hillside road.

f.w: the young man that kept the watch
f.g: A lookout posted on the city wall.

chapters.n: Jonadab points out the king’s sons arriving, just as he said.
The princes arrive weeping, and David and all his servants weep bitterly with them.
Absalom takes refuge with his grandfather, King Talmai of Geshur. David mourns every day — whether for Amnon or for his estranged son Absalom.
Absalom remains in Geshur for three years.

f.g: A small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee.

chapters.n: Over time David comes to terms with Amnon’s death and longs to see Absalom again. The Hebrew is uncertain; it may mean David’s anger toward Absalom faded.

f.w: longed to go forth unto Absalom
f.g: Some translations read “ceased to go out against Absalom” — his hostility eased.

chapters.n: Joab, ever the shrewd political operator, notices that David’s heart is drawn toward his exiled son Absalom, and he decides to engineer a reconciliation.

f.w: the king's heart was toward Absalom
f.g: The Hebrew could mean David’s thoughts were on Absalom, either with longing or with continued displeasure.

chapters.n: Joab brings a wise woman from Tekoah and asks her to act the part of a widow in long mourning.

f.g: A town in Judah about ten miles south of Jerusalem, later the hometown of the prophet Amos.
Pretend to be.
Mourners did not use perfumed oils, which were signs of everyday comfort and joy.

chapters.n: Joab gives her a script. Like Nathan’s parable, her story will lead David to judge a case that mirrors his own situation.

f.w: put the words in her mouth

chapters.n: She falls before the king and cries for help, as petitioners did when asking the king to judge their case.

f.g: Bowed down in respect.

chapters.n: She introduces herself as a widow — someone with no husband to protect her, one of those the law especially cared for.
Her story: her two sons fought in a field, and one killed the other. It parallels Absalom killing Amnon — and echoes Cain and Abel.

f.w: the one smote the other, and slew him

chapters.n: Now the family demands the surviving son’s death as blood vengeance. That would extinguish her last hope and erase her husband’s name and family line.

f.w: quench my coal which is left
f.g: Put out my last burning ember — a vivid image of her one remaining son and hope.
No name or descendant to carry on the family line.

chapters.n: David promises to look into the matter and protect her.
She offers to take any guilt on herself and her family, so the king will be free of blame if he spares her son.

f.g: Let any blame for sparing a killer fall on me.

chapters.n: David strengthens his promise: anyone who threatens her should be brought to him.
She asks David to swear by the Lord that the avenger of blood will not kill her son. He swears that not a hair of the boy’s head will be harmed — exactly the commitment she wanted.

f.g: The nearest relative who was to execute a murderer under ancient law.

f.w: not one hair of thy son fall to the earth

chapters.n: Having secured David’s oath, she asks permission to say one more thing.
Now she turns the case on him: if he would spare her son, why does he not bring back his own banished son? The whole nation suffers while its heir is in exile.

f.g: As one who is guilty — by his own ruling, David condemns his treatment of Absalom.
The one he has banished — Absalom.

chapters.n: Her most famous words: life is short, like water spilled on the ground that can’t be gathered up again. Yet God works to bring back those who are banished. Many readers see a beautiful picture of God’s plan to reconcile His estranged children.

f.w: as water spilt on the ground
f.g: Death is final and life is fleeting.

f.w: yet doth he devise means, that his banished be not expelled from him

chapters.n: She returns to her “own” story, claiming she came because people had frightened her.
She trusts the king will save her and her son from the man trying to cut them off from their inheritance in Israel.

f.g: Their family land and place among God’s covenant people.

chapters.n: She flatters David, saying his word will bring rest and that he discerns good and evil like an angel of God.

f.g: Comforting; bringing peace and rest.

chapters.n: David senses something behind all this and asks her to answer honestly.
He asks whether Joab is behind it, and she admits that Joab planned the whole thing and wrote her words.

f.g: Joab’s influence or involvement.

chapters.n: She says Joab wanted to change how the situation looked, and she praises David’s angel-like wisdom for seeing through it.

f.w: To fetch about this form of speech
f.g: To change the appearance of the matter — to approach it indirectly.

chapters.n: David gives in and tells Joab to bring Absalom home.

f.g: David’s tender phrase for his son; he uses it again in 2 Samuel 18:5.

chapters.n: Joab bows deeply and thanks the king, taking this as a sign of royal favor toward himself.
Joab goes to Geshur and brings Absalom back to Jerusalem.
But the reconciliation is only half-done: Absalom may live in Jerusalem but may not see the king’s face. This partial forgiveness leaves Absalom resentful.

f.w: let him not see my face
f.g: He was barred from the royal court and the king’s presence.

chapters.n: Absalom is famously handsome — flawless from head to toe. Like Saul, his impressive appearance hides deeper problems.
His thick hair is cut once a year and weighs about five pounds. This detail foreshadows how he will die.

f.g: Polled = cut the hair of.
About five pounds (2.3 kg).
The royal standard of weights.

chapters.n: Absalom has three sons and a daughter he names Tamar, after his wronged sister. The sons seem to have died young, since he later says he has no son to keep his name.
For two whole years Absalom lives in Jerusalem without seeing his father.
Absalom sends for Joab twice to arrange a meeting with the king, but Joab ignores him.
Absalom gets Joab’s attention by setting his barley field on fire — revealing a ruthless, impulsive streak.

f.g: Barley ripened in the spring; destroying a crop was a serious economic blow.

chapters.n: Now Joab comes, demanding to know why his field was burned.
Absalom complains he would have been better off in Geshur. He demands to see the king, and if he is guilty, to be executed — a bold challenge to his father.

f.w: if there be any iniquity in me, let him kill me
f.g: Absalom shows no remorse for killing Amnon.

chapters.n: Joab arranges the meeting. Absalom bows before David, and David kisses him — an outward reconciliation. But the next chapter shows that Absalom’s heart is far from reconciled.
Absalom begins to act like a king in waiting, riding in a chariot with fifty runners ahead of him — a public display of royal status.

f.w: fifty men to run before him
f.g: Runners in front of a chariot were a sign of royalty.

chapters.n: Every morning he stations himself by the city gate, where people came to have their legal cases heard by the king. He greets each one personally, asking where they are from.

f.g: The city gate was where legal and public business took place.
A legal dispute or lawsuit.

chapters.n: He tells each person that their case is good, but the king has no one to hear it — subtly blaming his father’s government for neglect.

f.g: Appointed, assigned.

chapters.n: “If only I were judge,” he says, “I would give everyone justice.” It is the oldest political tactic: promise everything and blame the current leader.

f.g: A legal case or complaint.

chapters.n: When people bow to him, Absalom instead takes their hand and kisses them, acting like their equal and friend.

f.g: A gesture of warm familiarity rather than royal distance.

chapters.n: In this way Absalom “stole the hearts” of Israel — winning loyalty through flattery and deception rather than true service.

f.g: Deceived them; won their affection dishonestly. Compare Genesis 31:20, where “stole away unawares” is literally “stole the heart.”

chapters.n: Absalom asks to go to Hebron to fulfill a religious vow. The “forty years” is likely a copying error; some ancient versions read “four years.”

f.g: Several ancient versions read “four years,” which fits the timeline better.
Absalom’s birthplace and David’s first capital — a symbolic place to claim the throne.

chapters.n: He claims he had promised to worship the Lord in Hebron if God brought him home. He uses religion as a cover for rebellion.
David sends him off with “Go in peace” — the last words he will ever speak to his son. The irony is painful.

f.g: Hebrew lek beshalom; the name Absalom means “father of peace.”

chapters.n: Absalom secretly sends agents throughout Israel, ready to proclaim him king at a trumpet signal.

f.g: Secret messengers or agents.

chapters.n: Two hundred guests from Jerusalem go with him innocently, unaware of the plot. Their presence makes it look as if leading citizens support Absalom.

f.g: Innocently, without knowing the plan.

chapters.n: Absalom recruits Ahithophel, David’s most trusted adviser — possibly Bath-sheba’s grandfather. The rebellion grows stronger by the day.

f.g: A town in the hill country of Judah.

chapters.n: A messenger brings David the alarming news: the people’s loyalty has shifted to Absalom.
David decides to flee Jerusalem at once, partly to spare the city from a bloody siege. He chooses retreat rather than fighting in the streets.

f.w: smite the city with the edge of the sword
f.g: David wished to protect Jerusalem’s people from violence.

chapters.n: David’s servants pledge their loyalty, ready to follow wherever he leads.
David leaves with his household, leaving ten concubines to care for the palace — a detail that will matter when Nathan’s prophecy is fulfilled.
The king and his people stop at “the far house,” perhaps the last house on the edge of the city.

f.w: a place that was far off
f.g: Literally “the far house” — possibly the last house before leaving the city.

chapters.n: His loyal troops march past him in review: the royal bodyguard and six hundred soldiers from Gath who had joined him.

f.w: the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites

f.g: Men from Gath, Philistine soldiers who had become loyal to David.

chapters.n: David urges Ittai, a Philistine newcomer, to go back and serve the new king rather than share David’s uncertain fate. He is a foreigner and owes David nothing.

f.w: a stranger, and also an exile
f.g: A foreigner who had already lost his own homeland.

chapters.n: David generously releases him: why should he wander with a fugitive king? He blesses him with steadfast love and faithfulness.

f.g: Ḥesed and ’emet — loyal love and faithfulness.

chapters.n: Ittai’s reply is one of the great statements of loyalty in scripture: wherever the king goes, in life or death, he will go too. A foreigner shows more faithfulness than David’s own son.

f.w: whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be

chapters.n: David accepts, and Ittai crosses over with all his men and their families.

f.g: Children and dependents.

chapters.n: The whole countryside weeps as the king crosses the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem toward the wilderness. Centuries later, Jesus would cross the same brook on the night of His betrayal.

f.g: A valley between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives.

chapters.n: The priests Zadok and Abiathar bring the ark with the Levites, setting it down until everyone has left the city.

f.w: the ark of the covenant of God

chapters.n: David sends the ark back. He will not use it as a good-luck charm; if God favors him, God will bring him back to see it again.

f.w: Carry back the ark of God into the city

f.g: His dwelling — the tent where the ark resided.

chapters.n: And if God has rejected him, David submits humbly: “Let him do to me as seemeth good.” His trust in God’s will is a model of meek faith.

f.w: let him do to me as seemeth good unto him

chapters.n: David asks Zadok, a seer, to return to Jerusalem with the two priests’ sons, who will serve as his messengers.

f.g: One who sees by revelation; or “Do you see?” — the Hebrew is debated.

chapters.n: David will wait by the fords of the Jordan in the wilderness until word arrives from them.

f.g: Inform me with reliable news.

chapters.n: The priests carry the ark back to Jerusalem and stay there.

David climbs the Mount of Olives weeping, head covered and barefoot, with all his people weeping too. The rejected king, betrayed by those close to him, going up Olivet in sorrow, foreshadows Jesus’ own suffering there.

f.g: The Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem across the Kidron.

f.w: had his head covered, and he went barefoot
f.g: Signs of mourning and humiliation.

chapters.n: When David learns his wise counselor Ahithophel has joined the conspiracy, he prays immediately that God will turn Ahithophel’s advice into foolishness.

f.w: turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness

chapters.n: At the summit, where people worshipped, David’s prayer begins to be answered: his friend Hushai arrives in mourning.

f.g: The Archites were a clan living near Bethel, on the border of Ephraim and Benjamin.

f.w: his coat rent, and earth upon his head

chapters.n: David tells Hushai, probably an older man, that he would only slow them down if he came along.
Instead, Hushai can serve him better by going back to Jerusalem, pretending loyalty to Absalom, and countering Ahithophel’s advice from the inside.

f.g: Defeat = frustrate, thwart.

chapters.n: Hushai can pass anything he learns to the priests Zadok and Abiathar.
Their sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan will carry messages to David — a network of loyal spies.
Hushai enters Jerusalem just as Absalom arrives. Both men reach the city at the same moment, and the contest of counsel is set to begin.

f.g: Possibly an official title, “the King’s Friend” — a trusted royal adviser (1 Chronicles 27:33).

chapters.n: Just past the summit of the Mount of Olives, Ziba, Mephibosheth’s steward, meets David with donkeys loaded with food and wine — a generous and well-timed gift.
