f.g: Probably cakes of figs or dates.
A wineskin.

chapters.n: Ziba explains that the donkeys are for the king’s family to ride, and the food and wine are for the weary travelers.

f.g: Weak, exhausted.

chapters.n: When David asks about Mephibosheth, Ziba claims his master stayed in Jerusalem hoping to get Saul’s kingdom back. Later Mephibosheth will deny this, so Ziba’s story may be a self-serving lie.

f.w: To day shall the house of Israel restore me the kingdom of my father

chapters.n: In a hasty decision made under stress, David gives all of Mephibosheth’s property to Ziba without hearing the other side. Ziba humbly thanks him.

f.w: thine are all that pertained unto Mephibosheth

chapters.n: At Bahurim, Shimei, a relative of Saul, comes out cursing David as he passes.
He throws stones at David and his men even though they are surrounded by armed guards — a bold act of hatred.

f.g: Throwing stones was a sign of contempt and a symbolic curse.

chapters.n: Shimei calls David a man of bloodshed and a worthless scoundrel.

f.g: A man guilty of shedding blood.
Belial = worthlessness; a wicked, good-for-nothing person.

chapters.n: He accuses David of taking Saul’s throne through violence and says God is now paying him back. The charge is unfair regarding Saul, though David did carry real guilt for Uriah’s blood.

f.w: all the blood of the house of Saul

f.g: Wickedness, evil.

chapters.n: Abishai, quick to violence like his brother Joab, asks permission to cut off Shimei’s head.
David rebukes Abishai. Perhaps the Lord has sent Shimei to curse him — who is David to stop it? David humbly accepts the rebuke as possibly deserved.

f.w: What have I to do with you
f.g: An idiom: “What do we have in common?” — “Stay out of this.”

chapters.n: If his own son wants him dead, why be surprised at a Benjamite’s anger? David chooses to leave Shimei alone.

f.w: my son, which came forth of my bowels
f.g: My own son, my own flesh and blood.
From the tribe of Benjamin, Saul’s tribe.

chapters.n: David hopes the Lord will see his suffering and turn the curse into a blessing. He trusts God to vindicate him rather than taking revenge.

f.w: the LORD will look on mine affliction

chapters.n: Shimei follows along the hillside, cursing, throwing stones, and flinging dust as David walks on in silence.

f.g: Throwing dust was a sign of contempt or a curse.

chapters.n: David and his weary followers finally reach a place to rest and refresh themselves, probably near the Jordan.

f.g: Some ancient versions read “came to the Jordan.”

chapters.n: Meanwhile Absalom enters Jerusalem with his supporters and his chief adviser, Ahithophel.
Hushai, David’s friend, greets Absalom with “Long live the king!” — carefully never saying which king.

f.g: Hebrew “May the king live!” — a royal acclamation (1 Samuel 10:24).

chapters.n: Absalom is suspicious and taunts Hushai for abandoning his friend David.

f.g: Ḥesed — loyal friendship.

chapters.n: Hushai’s answer is cleverly ambiguous: he will serve whomever the Lord and the people have chosen. Readers know the Lord’s chosen king is David.

f.w: whom the LORD, and this people, and all the men of Israel, choose

chapters.n: He says he will serve the son just as he served the father — words Absalom hears as loyalty.
Absalom asks Ahithophel for advice on what to do next.

Ahithophel advises Absalom to take his father’s concubines publicly. This would be a claim to David’s throne and an act so offensive that there could be no reconciliation, binding his followers to him.

f.w: Go in unto thy father's concubines

f.g: Made yourself hateful to your father — a complete break.

chapters.n: A tent is set up on the palace roof and Absalom does this publicly — on the very roof where David first saw Bath-sheba. Nathan’s prophecy is fulfilled exactly.

f.w: upon the top of the house
in the sight of all Israel

chapters.n: The narrator explains that Ahithophel’s advice was so respected that people treated it like a word from God. That makes the coming defeat of his counsel all the more remarkable.

f.g: Literally “the word of God” — as if inquiring of the Lord through a priest or prophet.

chapters.n: Ahithophel gives a sharp military plan: let him take twelve thousand men and chase David that very night, before David can regroup.
Striking while David is exhausted, he would scatter his followers and kill only the king — a quick, focused strike to avoid civil war.

f.g: Weary and discouraged.

f.w: I will smite the king only

chapters.n: With David dead, the people would return to Absalom and the nation would be at peace — like a bride returning to her husband, as some ancient versions put it.

f.w: the man whom thou seekest is as if all returned
f.g: The death of one man (David) would bring everyone back.

chapters.n: Absalom and Israel’s elders like the plan. It probably would have worked.
But Absalom wants a second opinion and summons Hushai — David’s secret agent. This is the answer to David’s prayer in 2 Samuel 15:31.

f.w: Call now Hushai the Archite also

chapters.n: Absalom explains Ahithophel’s plan and asks Hushai whether they should follow it.
Hushai boldly contradicts the famous counselor, but tactfully: Ahithophel’s advice is just “not good at this time.”
He plays on Absalom’s fear: David and his men are hardened warriors, as fierce as a mother bear robbed of her cubs. A veteran like David won’t be caught sleeping among his troops.

f.g: Bitter, enraged.

f.w: a bear robbed of her whelps
f.g: Whelps = cubs.

chapters.n: David is surely hiding somewhere, Hushai warns. If Absalom’s forces suffer early losses, panic will spread among them.

f.g: A cave or ravine.

chapters.n: Even the bravest of Absalom’s men would lose heart, knowing David’s reputation.

f.g: Lose all courage.

chapters.n: Hushai advises gathering a massive army from all Israel, with Absalom leading it personally — flattering his vanity and buying David time.

f.w: as the sand that is by the sea for multitude

f.g: Personally leading the army.

chapters.n: With overwhelming numbers they would cover David like dew on the ground and leave no survivors — a grand and vivid picture designed to impress.

f.g: Fall upon, descend on.

chapters.n: Even if David hides in a city, all Israel could drag it into a valley with ropes. The exaggeration appeals to Absalom’s pride.

f.g: Or “the valley.”

chapters.n: Absalom and his men choose Hushai’s advice. The narrator reveals why: the Lord had arranged to defeat Ahithophel’s good counsel in order to bring disaster on Absalom.

f.w: the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel

chapters.n: Hushai immediately reports both plans to the priests Zadok and Abiathar.
He urges that David cross the Jordan tonight, in case Absalom changes his mind and follows Ahithophel’s plan.

f.g: Destroyed completely.

chapters.n: The priests’ sons wait at a spring outside the city to avoid notice. A servant girl brings them the message, and they set off to David.

f.g: A spring just south of Jerusalem in the Kidron Valley.
A maidservant, servant girl (no negative meaning in KJV English).

chapters.n: A boy spots them and tells Absalom. The messengers hurry to a house in Bahurim and hide in a well in its courtyard.

f.g: Courtyard.

chapters.n: The woman of the house covers the well and spreads grain over it, hiding the young men. The scene recalls Rahab hiding the spies.

f.g: Crushed grain, spread out as if to dry.

f.w: spread a covering over the well's mouth

chapters.n: When Absalom’s men come, she misdirects them, and they give up and return to Jerusalem.

f.g: The meaning of this Hebrew word is uncertain.

chapters.n: The messengers climb out and rush to warn David to cross the Jordan quickly.
David leads all his people across the Jordan during the night; by morning, not one is left behind.

When his advice is rejected, Ahithophel foresees Absalom’s defeat. He goes home, puts his affairs in order, and takes his own life. Many see a parallel with Judas, the trusted friend who betrayed Jesus and then hanged himself.
David reaches Mahanaim, east of the Jordan — the same town that was Ish-bosheth’s capital. Absalom crosses the Jordan with all Israel to pursue him.
Absalom makes his cousin Amasa army commander instead of Joab. Amasa is also related to David, which makes this a family civil war.

f.g: Not David’s wife Abigail, but his sister or half-sister.

chapters.n: Absalom’s army camps in Gilead, east of the Jordan.

f.g: The highland region east of the Jordan River.

chapters.n: At Mahanaim, three unexpected friends come to help David: an Ammonite prince, the man who once sheltered Mephibosheth, and an aged wealthy Gileadite.
They bring bedding, bowls, pottery, and all kinds of grain and beans — generous supplies for weary refugees.

f.g: Roasted grain.
Lentils, beans, and other edible seeds.

chapters.n: They also bring honey, curds, sheep, and cheese, recognizing that David’s people were hungry, tired, and thirsty. In his darkest hour, God sends David friends.

f.g: Kine = cows; cheese from cows’ milk.
Probably curds or yogurt.

chapters.n: At Mahanaim, David organizes his loyal forces — now swelled by new arrivals — into units of thousands and hundreds, each with an officer.

f.g: Counted and organized for battle.

chapters.n: He divides the army into three divisions under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, the loyal Philistine. David plans to lead them himself.
The troops refuse to let him go. The enemy is really after David; he is worth ten thousand of them, so he should support them from the city.

f.w: thou art worth ten thousand of us

f.g: Help us, send us reinforcements.

chapters.n: David agrees and stands at the city gate as his army marches out in its units.
In the hearing of the whole army, David commands his generals to be gentle with Absalom for his sake. Even now, his father’s heart wants to save his rebellious son.

f.w: Deal gently for my sake with the young man

chapters.n: The battle takes place in the forest of Ephraim, probably a wooded area east of the Jordan in Gilead.

f.g: A forest in Gilead, probably named for Ephraimite settlers or an earlier event (Judges 12:1-6).

chapters.n: Absalom’s army is routed by David’s experienced men, and twenty thousand fall.
The battle spreads through rugged terrain, and the forest — with its ravines, thickets, and pits — kills more men than swords do. Nature itself seems to fight for David.

f.g: Many died from the dangerous terrain while fleeing.

chapters.n: Fleeing on his royal mule, Absalom gets his head caught in the branches of a large oak and is left hanging in the air as the mule runs on. His pride — perhaps his famous hair — becomes his trap.

f.w: his head caught hold of the oak

f.g: The royal riding animal; losing it symbolizes losing the kingdom.

chapters.n: A soldier sees him and reports to Joab.
Joab demands to know why the man didn’t kill Absalom on the spot, saying he would have rewarded him.

f.w: ten shekels of silver, and a girdle
f.g: About four ounces of silver and a soldier’s belt — a reward and honor.

chapters.n: The soldier refuses: not even for a thousand shekels would he harm the king’s son, since David had commanded them all to protect Absalom.

f.w: Beware that none touch the young man Absalom

chapters.n: He adds that if he had done it, the king would have found out — and Joab would have abandoned him to take the blame.

f.w: wrought falsehood against mine own life
f.g: Acted treacherously at the risk of my own life.

chapters.n: Joab won’t waste time. He takes three spears or sticks and drives them into Absalom while he hangs in the tree. Joab disobeys the king, judging that Absalom alive was too dangerous.

f.g: Probably clubs, sticks, or short spears.

chapters.n: Joab’s ten armor-bearers surround Absalom and finish him off.
With Absalom dead, Joab sounds the trumpet to stop the fighting. The rebellion is over, and there is no need to kill more Israelites.
They throw Absalom’s body into a pit and cover it with a large heap of stones — a burial of shame, like those of Israel’s condemned enemies.

f.w: a very great heap of stones

chapters.n: The contrast is striking: Absalom had built himself a monument in the King’s Valley because he had no son to carry his name. He wanted honor, but ended in a pit under stones.

f.g: A standing stone monument; the so-called “Absalom’s Tomb” in Jerusalem’s Kidron Valley was built much later.
Dale = valley.

chapters.n: Ahimaaz, the priest’s son, eagerly asks to run to David with the “good news” of victory.
Joab refuses. News of the death of the king’s son is not good news for David, and messengers with bad news could suffer.

f.w: because the king's son is dead

chapters.n: Joab sends a Cushite instead — a foreign servant who would deliver the news plainly.

f.g: “The Cushite” — a man from Cush (Ethiopia/Nubia).

chapters.n: Ahimaaz begs again to run. Joab asks why, since he has no message worth any reward.
Ahimaaz insists, and Joab finally lets him go. He takes the easier route through the Jordan plain and outruns the Cushite.

f.g: The Jordan valley route — longer but flatter and faster.
Outran, passed.

chapters.n: David sits between the inner and outer gates of the city, waiting anxiously for news. A watchman climbs up and sees a lone runner.

f.g: City gates often had an inner and outer gate with a chamber between them.

chapters.n: David reasons that a single runner must be a messenger; a fleeing army would come as a crowd.

f.g: Quickly.

chapters.n: Then a second runner appears. David hopes he too brings news.

f.g: Gatekeeper.

chapters.n: The watchman recognizes Ahimaaz by his running style, and David is reassured that a good man must bring good news.
Ahimaaz cries out “Shalom!” — all is well — and praises God for delivering the king from his enemies.

f.g: Hebrew shalom — peace, well-being.

chapters.n: David’s first question is not about the battle but about his son. Ahimaaz avoids the truth and claims he only saw a commotion.

f.w: Is the young man Absalom safe?
f.g: Literally “Is there shalom for the young man Absalom?”
Uproar, commotion.

chapters.n: David tells him to step aside and wait.
The Cushite arrives and announces that the Lord has avenged the king of all who rose against him.

f.g: Vindicated you; given you justice.

chapters.n: David asks the same question. The Cushite answers diplomatically, wishing that all the king’s enemies might share Absalom’s fate — and David understands his son is dead.

David breaks down, climbs to the room above the gate, and weeps: “O my son Absalom… would God I had died for thee.” His cry reveals a father’s love for a son who had tried to kill him. Many see in it a glimpse of God’s own love for His wayward children — love that in Christ was willing to die for them.

f.w: would God I had died for thee
f.g: An expression meaning “If only I had died instead of you.”

chapters.n: Word reaches Joab that the king is weeping and mourning for Absalom.
The army’s victory turns into a day of mourning as the soldiers hear of the king’s grief.
The soldiers slip quietly into the city as if they had lost the battle and were ashamed.

f.g: Quietly, secretly.

chapters.n: David covers his face and keeps crying aloud for his son.

f.g: A sign of deep mourning.

chapters.n: Joab confronts David bluntly: his grief is shaming the very men who risked their lives to save him and his family.

f.g: You have humiliated.

chapters.n: Joab accuses David of loving his enemies and hating his friends, as if he would rather have Absalom alive and all his loyal soldiers dead.

f.g: Joab means this as a rebuke, though Jesus would later teach a higher form of love for enemies (Matthew 5:44).

chapters.n: Joab warns that unless David goes out and speaks kindly to his troops at once, they will desert him that very night — a worse disaster than anything he has faced.

f.g: Speak kindly; literally “speak to the heart.”

chapters.n: David puts aside his grief and takes his seat at the city gate, where kings received their people. The soldiers come before him.

f.g: The public place for the king to appear and hold court.

chapters.n: Across the tribes, people argue: David had saved them from the Philistines, yet they had let him be driven out by Absalom.

f.g: Arguing, debating.

chapters.n: With Absalom, whom they had anointed, now dead, people ask why no one is moving to bring King David back.

f.w: Absalom, whom we anointed over us
f.g: Absalom had been anointed king by his supporters.

chapters.n: David sends word through the priests to Judah’s elders: why is his own tribe the last to bring him home? He uses diplomacy rather than force.

f.w: Zadok and to Abiathar the priests

chapters.n: He reminds Judah that they are his own kin.
In a bold move, David offers Amasa — Absalom’s former commander — the command of his army in place of Joab. This wins over the rebels and demotes Joab for killing Absalom.

f.g: In place of Joab.

chapters.n: Judah responds as one man, inviting the king and his followers to return.

f.g: He won them over.

chapters.n: David comes back to the Jordan, and Judah gathers at Gilgal to escort him across.

f.g: A historic site near Jericho where Israel first camped in the land and where Saul’s kingship was renewed.

chapters.n: Shimei, who had cursed David, hurries down with the men of Judah to meet him.
He brings a thousand Benjaminites with him, and Ziba and his household also rush across the river to meet the king.
A ferry carries the king’s household over. Shimei falls before David as he crosses.

f.g: The Hebrew may mean a crossing or ford; the exact meaning is uncertain.

chapters.n: Shimei begs David not to hold his earlier sin against him.

f.g: Count it as guilt; hold it against me.
Wickedly, wrongly.

chapters.n: He admits his sin and points out he is the first of the northern tribes to come and welcome the king.

f.g: Here a name for the northern tribes in general, including Benjamin.

chapters.n: Abishai again wants Shimei killed for cursing the Lord’s anointed king.
David refuses. This is a day of restoration, not revenge; no Israelite will be executed today.

f.g: Opponents; the Hebrew word is satan, meaning one who stands in the way.

f.w: shall there any man be put to death this day in Israel?

chapters.n: David swears that Shimei will not die. (Later, David’s final instructions to Solomon will revisit Shimei’s case.)
Mephibosheth comes to meet David. He has not cared for his feet, trimmed his beard, or washed his clothes since David fled — outward signs of genuine mourning and loyalty.

f.g: Cared for his feet; possibly trimmed his toenails.

chapters.n: David asks why he didn’t come along when the king fled.

f.g: Why.

chapters.n: Mephibosheth explains that he is lame and needed a donkey saddled, but his servant Ziba deceived him and went without him.
Ziba had slandered him, he says, but he trusts the king to act wisely, like an angel of God.

f.g: Told lies about.

chapters.n: He humbly acknowledges that Saul’s family deserved nothing, yet David gave him a place at his table. He asks for nothing more.

f.g: Men deserving death — doomed.

chapters.n: David, unable to know who is telling the truth, divides the land between Mephibosheth and Ziba.

f.w: Thou and Ziba divide the land

chapters.n: Mephibosheth replies that Ziba can have it all — what matters is that the king has returned safely. His response suggests his loyalty was sincere.
Barzillai, the wealthy elderly Gileadite who had supplied David, comes to escort the king across the Jordan.
Barzillai is eighty years old and had generously provided for David at Mahanaim.

f.g: Fourscore = 80.
A very wealthy and important man.

chapters.n: David invites him to live in Jerusalem at the king’s expense, as a reward.
Barzillai gently declines, noting his advanced age.
At eighty, he says, he can hardly enjoy fine food, drink, or music anymore. Why burden the king? His words give a touching, honest picture of old age.
He will go a little way with the king, but needs no reward for that.

f.g: Repay, reward.

chapters.n: Barzillai asks to die at home near his parents’ graves, and offers Chimham, probably his son, to go with the king instead.
David agrees to take Chimham and promises to grant Barzillai any request.
After the crossing, David kisses and blesses Barzillai, who returns home.
David proceeds to Gilgal, escorted by all of Judah but only half of Israel — a sign of tension to come.
The northern tribes complain that Judah has “stolen” the king by escorting him back without them.

f.g: Taken you secretly, without including us.

chapters.n: Judah replies that David is their close relative, and they have received no special favors from him.

f.g: A close relative; David was from the tribe of Judah.

chapters.n: The northern tribes argue they have ten shares in the king and a greater right to him. But Judah’s words are even harsher. This bitter rivalry sets up Sheba’s revolt and, generations later, the division of the kingdom.

f.g: Ten tribes, versus Judah’s one (Benjamin and Simeon being counted with others in different ways).

chapters.n: The tribal quarrel at the end of chapter 19 explodes. Sheba, a troublemaker from Saul’s tribe of Benjamin, sounds the trumpet and calls the northern tribes to abandon David.

f.g: A worthless, wicked man.

f.w: We have no part in David
f.g: Almost the same cry will split the kingdom after Solomon’s death.
A call to go home — to withdraw support from the king.

chapters.n: The northern tribes follow Sheba, but Judah stays loyal and escorts David from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

f.g: Clave = clung to, stayed loyal to.

chapters.n: Back in Jerusalem, David places the ten concubines Absalom had violated under guard, providing for them but no longer living with them as wives. They spend their lives like widows — further victims of the family’s tragedy.

f.g: Kept them in a guarded house.

chapters.n: David orders his new commander Amasa to gather Judah’s troops within three days.
Amasa takes longer than the time set — perhaps because Judah’s men were slow to follow Absalom’s former general.
Fearing Sheba will grow more dangerous than Absalom, David sends Abishai with the royal troops to chase him before he reaches fortified cities.

f.g: Walled, fortified cities.

chapters.n: Joab’s men, the royal guard, and the elite warriors set out from Jerusalem. Joab joins them, though he is no longer officially in command.
At Gibeon, Amasa meets them. Joab arranges his sword so that it falls out of its sheath — likely a deliberate trick to have it in his hand without suspicion.

f.w: the great stone which is in Gibeon
f.g: A landmark rock at Gibeon, near where Joab fought Abner (2 Samuel 2:12-17).

chapters.n: Joab greets Amasa warmly, calling him “my brother” and taking his beard as if to kiss him — a customary greeting.

f.w: Art thou in health, my brother?
f.g: Literally “Is it shalom with you?”

chapters.n: Amasa doesn’t notice the sword in Joab’s other hand, and Joab kills him with one stroke — exactly as he had killed Abner. Then Joab simply resumes command and pursues Sheba.

f.g: He needed only one blow.

chapters.n: One of Joab’s men calls everyone to follow Joab if they support David — linking loyalty to the king with loyalty to Joab.
Amasa’s body lies in the road, stopping the troops in their tracks. The soldier drags it into a field and covers it with a cloth.

f.g: Lay in his own blood.

chapters.n: With the body out of sight, the army moves on after Joab.
Sheba travels through the northern tribes to Abel Beth-maachah in the far north, gathering his own clan along the way.

f.g: Abel Beth-maachah, a fortified town near Dan in northern Israel.
Possibly the Bichrites — Sheba’s own clan.

chapters.n: Joab besieges the city, building a siege ramp and battering the wall.

f.g: Built an earthen siege ramp up to the wall.

chapters.n: A wise woman calls from the wall, asking to speak with Joab.
She confirms she is speaking to Joab and asks him to listen.

f.g: Servant woman — a polite way of referring to herself.

chapters.n: She reminds him that Abel was famous for wisdom: people used to say, “Ask advice at Abel,” and disputes were settled there.

f.g: Were wont = used to; it was customary to say.

chapters.n: She speaks for her peaceful, loyal city. Why destroy a “mother in Israel” — a major town — and part of the Lord’s inheritance?

f.g: A leading city with dependent villages around it.
God’s land and people.

chapters.n: Joab insists he has no desire to destroy the city.

f.g: God forbid; certainly not.

chapters.n: He only wants Sheba, the rebel. Hand him over and the army will leave. The woman promises Sheba’s head will be thrown over the wall.

f.g: The hill country of Ephraim, which included parts of Benjamin.

chapters.n: Through her wisdom, the townspeople execute Sheba and give his head to Joab. One woman’s counsel saves a whole city. Joab sounds the trumpet and returns to Jerusalem.
Joab is again commander of the army — having regained his post by murder. A list of David’s officials follows.
Adoram oversees forced labor — a new office that shows the kingdom’s growing demands on its people.

f.g: Tribute here = forced labor; also called Adoniram.

chapters.n: Sheva serves as secretary, and Zadok and Abiathar as the priests.

f.g: Probably the same official as Seraiah in 2 Samuel 8:17.

chapters.n: Ira the Jairite serves as a priest or chief official for David.

f.g: Hebrew kohen, normally “priest”; perhaps a personal priest or royal adviser.

chapters.n: Chapters 21–24 form an appendix of events from various times in David’s reign. A three-year famine strikes, and when David seeks the Lord, he learns it is because Saul broke Israel’s covenant with the Gibeonites by killing them.

f.g: A family guilty of shedding innocent blood.

chapters.n: The narrator explains: the Gibeonites were not Israelites but survivors of the Amorites, protected by an oath Israel made in Joshua’s day. Saul, in misguided zeal, tried to wipe them out.

f.w: the children of Israel had sworn unto them

f.g: A general name for the pre-Israelite peoples of Canaan.

chapters.n: David asks the Gibeonites what he can do to make amends so that they will bless the land instead of having cause to curse it.

f.g: Here, making things right — repairing a broken covenant.

chapters.n: They refuse money and do not claim the right to kill just any Israelite. David promises to do whatever they ask.

f.w: We will have no silver nor gold

chapters.n: They identify Saul as the man who tried to exterminate them from all Israel’s territory.

f.g: Coasts = borders, territory.

chapters.n: They ask for seven of Saul’s descendants to be executed at Saul’s hometown. It reflects the ancient view of collective family guilt — a harsh custom that later scripture moved away from.

f.w: hang them up unto the LORD
f.g: The Hebrew suggests executing and exposing the bodies, perhaps by impaling or dismembering.

chapters.n: David protects Mephibosheth, honoring his sacred oath to Jonathan. Here two covenants are kept: Israel’s with Gibeon and David’s with Jonathan.

f.w: the LORD's oath that was between them

chapters.n: He hands over two sons of Saul’s concubine Rizpah and five grandsons through Saul’s daughter. Most manuscripts say Michal, but the woman married to Adriel was her sister Merab, so many translations read Merab.

f.g: Merab, Michal’s older sister, was married to Adriel; a copyist may have confused the names.
Bore, or raised.

chapters.n: The seven are executed together at Gibeah at the start of barley harvest, in early spring.

f.g: Around April, the first harvest of the year.

chapters.n: Rizpah, a grieving mother, spreads sackcloth on the rock and keeps vigil over the bodies for months, driving away birds and wild animals until the rains come. Her quiet, faithful love is one of the most moving scenes in the book.

f.w: until water dropped upon them out of heaven
f.g: Until the autumn rains — possibly a signal that the famine had ended.
Suffered = allowed.

chapters.n: David hears what Rizpah has done.
Moved by her devotion, David retrieves the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead, whose men had rescued them from the Philistines.

f.w: stolen them from the street of Beth-shan

chapters.n: He gathers their bones along with those of the seven who were executed.
They are all buried with honor in Saul’s family tomb in Benjamin. After this, God answers prayer for the land. Covenant faithfulness and respect for the dead bring healing.

f.w: the sepulchre of Kish his father
God was entreated for the land
f.g: God responded to prayers and ended the famine.

chapters.n: Several accounts of battles with Philistine giants follow. In one, David grows exhausted in battle.

f.g: Grew weary, worn out.

chapters.n: A giant named Ishbi-benob, armed with a huge bronze spearhead and a new sword, tries to kill the tired David.

f.g: Possibly descendants of Rapha, ancestor of the giant Rephaim, or members of an elite warrior group.
About 7.5 pounds (3.4 kg) — half the weight of Goliath’s spearhead (1 Samuel 17:7).

chapters.n: Abishai rescues David. His men swear David must never again go to battle, lest Israel’s “lamp” be extinguished.

f.g: The king was the lamp of the nation; his life kept the people’s hope burning.

chapters.n: In another battle at Gob, Sibbechai kills another giant named Saph.

f.g: An unidentified place, perhaps near Gezer (1 Chronicles 20:4).

chapters.n: Elhanan kills Goliath’s brother, who carried a spear as thick as a weaver’s beam. The words “the brother of” are added by the translators; 1 Chronicles explains he killed Lahmi, Goliath’s brother.

f.g: The thick wooden rod on a loom.

chapters.n: At Gath, a giant with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot appears.
When he taunts Israel, as Goliath once did, David’s nephew Jonathan kills him.
These four giants of Gath were defeated by David and his men. David’s early victory over Goliath finds its echo in the victories of those he trained.
This song of praise appears again, with small differences, as Psalm 18. David looks back over a lifetime of rescues — from Saul and from every enemy — and gives God the credit.
David piles up images of safety: God is his rock, his fortress, his rescuer. A man who often hid in rocky strongholds knew that his true protection was the Lord.

f.g: A mountain stronghold, like the ones where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 23:14).

chapters.n: More titles follow: shield, horn of salvation, high tower, refuge, and Savior. Zacharias later used “horn of salvation” for the coming Messiah.

f.g: A horn symbolized strength, like the horns of a powerful animal.

chapters.n: David’s life lesson in one line: call on the Lord, and you will be saved.

f.w: I will call on the LORD

chapters.n: He describes past dangers as crashing waves of death and torrents of wicked men.

f.g: Compassed = surrounded.
Hebrew belial — worthlessness, destruction.

chapters.n: The cords of the grave were wrapped around him, and death’s traps confronted him.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the place of the dead, the grave.
Prevented = came before me, confronted me (not “stopped”).

chapters.n: In his distress he cried out, and God heard him from His heavenly temple. The rest of the song describes the answer.

f.w: he did hear my voice out of his temple

chapters.n: God’s response is pictured as a mighty storm and earthquake — the language of a theophany, God appearing in power as He did at Sinai.

f.g: Angry — here, God’s righteous anger at those harming His servant.

chapters.n: Smoke and fire pour from Him — poetic images of His overwhelming power, like a volcano or lightning storm.
He tears open the heavens and descends, with dark storm clouds beneath His feet. God comes down to rescue His servant.

f.w: He bowed the heavens also, and came down

chapters.n: He rides on a cherub and soars on the wind — pictures of a God who moves swiftly to help.

f.g: Psalm 18:10 reads “he did fly,” a very similar Hebrew word.

chapters.n: He surrounds Himself with darkness and heavy rain clouds like a royal tent.

f.g: Tents or canopies.

chapters.n: Out of the brightness of His presence, burning coals blaze — likely a description of lightning.
The Lord thunders from heaven; the Most High speaks with a mighty voice.

f.g: Hebrew ‘Elyon — a title for God as supreme over all.

chapters.n: His lightning bolts are like arrows, scattering David’s enemies.

f.g: Discomfited = threw into confusion, routed.

chapters.n: At His rebuke the sea bed and the foundations of the earth are laid bare — recalling the parting of the Red Sea.

f.w: the channels of the sea appeared

f.g: Discovered = uncovered, laid bare.

chapters.n: The God of the storm reaches down and personally pulls David out of deep waters. The vast cosmic power is directed toward one person in need.

f.w: he drew me out of many waters

chapters.n: He saves David from powerful enemies who were too strong for him alone.

f.w: they were too strong for me

chapters.n: Enemies confronted him in his worst moment, but the Lord was his support.

f.g: Stay = support, something to lean on.

chapters.n: God brought him into a wide-open space — freedom after confinement — because He delighted in him.

f.g: Open, spacious ground — a picture of freedom and safety.

chapters.n: David says God rewarded his righteousness. These words likely come from earlier years, before his great sin — or speak of his overall faithfulness and loyalty to God, in contrast to Saul.

f.g: Innocence of wrongdoing.

chapters.n: He kept the Lord’s ways and did not turn from God to idols.

f.g: Turned away from God in rebellion.

chapters.n: God’s laws were always before him as his guide.

f.g: God’s decisions and laws.
Fixed laws and decrees.

chapters.n: He kept himself blameless before God and guarded against sin.

f.g: Hebrew tamim — whole, complete, wholehearted.

chapters.n: So, he repeats, God has rewarded him according to his righteousness.

f.g: Repaid, rewarded.

chapters.n: A key principle: God deals with people according to their character. The merciful find mercy, the blameless find integrity.

f.w: With the merciful thou wilt shew thyself merciful

chapters.n: With the pure, God shows Himself pure; with the crooked, He shows Himself shrewd — He outmaneuvers their schemes.

f.g: Froward = perverse, crooked.
Twisted, shrewd — God matches their crookedness with His cleverness.

chapters.n: God rescues the humble but brings down the proud.

f.w: the afflicted people thou wilt save

f.g: Proud, arrogant.

chapters.n: The Lord is David’s lamp, turning his darkness to light.

f.w: thou art my lamp, O LORD

chapters.n: With God’s strength he can charge an enemy band and leap over a city wall — nothing can stop him.

f.g: A raiding band of soldiers.

chapters.n: God’s way is perfect; His word is proven true; He shields all who trust Him.

f.w: the word of the LORD is tried
f.g: Tried = refined like metal, proven pure.
A small shield.

chapters.n: Who is God except the Lord? Who is a rock except our God? He alone is worthy of trust.

f.w: who is a rock, save our God?

chapters.n: God is his strong refuge and clears his path.

f.g: Psalm 18:32 reads “He girdeth me with strength, and maketh my way perfect.”

chapters.n: God makes his feet sure like a deer’s on steep mountain heights.

f.g: Hinds = female deer, known for sure-footedness on rocky slopes.

chapters.n: God trains him for battle so that he can bend even a bronze bow.

f.g: Literally a bow of bronze — a very stiff, powerful bow.

chapters.n: God’s saving shield protected him, and God’s gentle condescension made him great. The Lord stoops down to lift people up.

f.w: thy gentleness hath made me great
f.g: Or “your humility” — God’s willingness to stoop down to help.

chapters.n: God widened his path so his feet would not slip.

f.g: Gave him room to walk securely.

chapters.n: David pursued and destroyed his enemies completely.
They fell beneath his feet and could not rise again.
God equipped him with strength for battle and subdued his attackers.

f.g: Girded = wrapped or equipped, as with a belt.

chapters.n: God made his enemies turn their backs and flee.

f.w: given me the necks of mine enemies
f.g: Made them turn their backs (necks) to me in retreat.

chapters.n: His enemies cried for help, even to the Lord, but no one answered — they had not been faithful to Him.
He crushed them like dust and trampled them like street mud.

f.g: Mud.

chapters.n: God delivered him from conflicts among his own people and made him ruler over foreign nations too.

f.g: Rebellions and quarrels within Israel, such as Absalom’s and Sheba’s.
Here simply other nations, non-Israelites.

chapters.n: Foreigners come cringing to submit as soon as they hear of him.

f.g: Foreigners.

chapters.n: They lose heart and come trembling out of their strongholds.

f.g: Fortresses, hiding places.

chapters.n: A burst of praise: the Lord lives! David blesses God, his rock and Savior.
It is God who gives him vengeance and subdues nations — not David’s own strength.

f.w: It is God that avengeth me

chapters.n: God lifted him above his attackers and saved him from violent men.
So David will praise the Lord among the nations. Paul quotes this verse to show that the gospel was always meant for the Gentiles too.

f.w: I will give thanks unto thee, O LORD, among the heathen

chapters.n: The song ends with God’s faithful love to His anointed king, David, and his descendants forever — pointing back to the covenant of chapter 7 and forward to Christ, the “Anointed One” from David’s line.

f.g: Hebrew mashiach — Messiah, “anointed one.”

chapters.n: These are David’s “last words” — perhaps his final poetic testimony. He describes himself as a shepherd’s son raised high by God, anointed king, and Israel’s beloved singer of psalms.

f.g: Or “the favorite of the songs of Israel” — the one Israel loved to sing about, or Israel’s pleasant singer.

chapters.n: David testifies that his words came by inspiration: the Spirit of the Lord spoke through him. Jesus and the apostles also taught that David spoke by the Holy Ghost.

f.w: The Spirit of the LORD spake by me

chapters.n: God’s message to him concerns the ideal ruler: one who governs justly and in reverence for God.

f.w: He that ruleth over men must be just

f.g: Reverent awe and obedience toward God.

chapters.n: Such a ruler is like a cloudless sunrise, or like fresh grass sparkling after rain — bringing life and blessing to his people. Christians see the perfect fulfillment in Jesus Christ.

f.w: as the light of the morning
the tender grass springing out of the earth

chapters.n: David admits his own house has not always been righteous, yet God has made an everlasting covenant with him, secure in every detail. This covenant is his whole hope.

f.w: ordered in all things, and sure
f.g: Carefully arranged and guaranteed.

f.w: although he make it not to grow
f.g: The Hebrew can also be read as a question: “Will He not make it grow?” — an expression of confidence.

chapters.n: In contrast, the wicked are like thorns that are thrown away — too prickly to grab with bare hands.

f.g: Worthless, wicked people.

chapters.n: Thorns are handled with iron tools and burned up on the spot — a picture of how evildoers will finally be removed.

f.g: Armed, equipped.

chapters.n: The chapter now honors David’s elite warriors. First is Josheb-basshebeth (called the Tachmonite and Adino), the chief of the Three, who killed eight hundred in one fight.

f.w: The Tachmonite that sat in the seat
f.g: The Hebrew is difficult; 1 Chronicles 11:11 names him Jashobeam the Hachmonite.
Chronicles gives 300.

chapters.n: Second of the Three is Eleazar, who stood with David against the Philistines when Israel’s army retreated.
He fought until his hand cramped and stuck to his sword. The narrator credits the Lord for the victory; the rest of the army came back only to collect the spoil.

f.w: his hand clave unto the sword
f.g: Clave = stuck; his grip had frozen from exhaustion.

f.w: the LORD wrought a great victory

chapters.n: Third is Shammah. When the people fled from the Philistines in a lentil field, he did not.

f.g: Possibly “the mountaineer,” from the hill country.
A field of lentils — food for the people.

chapters.n: He stood his ground alone in the middle of the field and defended it. Again, the Lord gave the victory. Sometimes faithfulness means holding firm where you are.

f.w: he stood in the midst of the ground

chapters.n: A story from David’s early outlaw days: three of the Thirty come to him at the cave of Adullam while the Philistines occupy the valley near Jerusalem.
David is in his stronghold, and a Philistine garrison holds his hometown of Bethlehem.

f.g: A stronghold or fortress.

chapters.n: Homesick, David wishes aloud for a drink from the well by Bethlehem’s gate, the water of his childhood.

f.g: Perhaps a cistern near the town gate.

chapters.n: His three warriors break through enemy lines and bring him the water. But David refuses to drink it and pours it out as an offering to the Lord.

f.w: poured it out unto the LORD
f.g: A drink offering — giving to God something too precious to keep for oneself.

chapters.n: David says drinking it would be like drinking the blood of men who risked their lives. He honors their sacrifice by giving it to God. Their loyalty and his reverence both shine here.

f.w: the blood of the men that went in jeopardy of their lives
f.g: Jeopardy = danger.

chapters.n: Abishai, Joab’s brother, led another group of three and once killed three hundred men with his spear.

f.g: Some manuscripts read “chief of the thirty.”

chapters.n: He was honored and became their commander, though he did not rank with the first Three.

f.g: Did not equal; did not reach the rank of.

chapters.n: Benaiah, a valiant man from Kabzeel in southern Judah, did many deeds: he killed two of Moab’s great warriors and, on a snowy day, killed a lion in a pit.

f.g: The Hebrew ’ari’el is unclear: great champions, or perhaps “the two sons of Ariel.”

chapters.n: He also faced a huge Egyptian armed with a spear, using only a club. He snatched the spear and killed the man with his own weapon — echoing David’s defeat of Goliath.

f.g: An impressive, large man; 1 Chronicles 11:23 says he was five cubits (about 7.5 feet) tall.

f.w: slew him with his own spear

chapters.n: These deeds made Benaiah famous alongside the Three.
Benaiah was honored above the Thirty, though not among the Three. David made him commander of his personal bodyguard; he later became Solomon’s army commander.
The roster of the Thirty begins. Asahel heads the list, though he died early in David’s reign — a mark of honor. Elhanan of Bethlehem was from David’s hometown.

f.g: A different man from the Elhanan in 2 Samuel 21:19.

chapters.n: Two warriors from Harod, perhaps near the spring where Gideon chose his three hundred.

f.g: From Harod, possibly a town in Judah or near the spring of Harod.

chapters.n: Helez came from Beth-pelet in southern Judah, and Ira from Tekoa — the hometown of the wise woman and, later, of Amos.
Abiezer came from Anathoth, a priestly town in Benjamin that would later be Jeremiah’s home. Mebunnai came from Hushah in Judah.

f.g: Likely the same man as Sibbechai the Hushathite; the names look alike in Hebrew.

chapters.n: Zalmon was of the Ahohite clan, like Eleazar of the Three. Maharai came from Netophah, a village near Bethlehem.

f.g: From Netophah, close to Bethlehem.

chapters.n: Heleb was another Netophathite. This Ittai (not the Philistine Ittai) was from Gibeah of Benjamin — Saul’s own hometown, showing that some Benjaminites were loyal to David.

f.g: Different from Ittai the Gittite in 2 Samuel 15:19.

f.w: Gibeah of the children of Benjamin

chapters.n: This Benaiah came from Pirathon in Ephraim, the hometown of the judge Abdon. Hiddai came from the ravines of Mount Gaash, near Joshua’s burial place.
Abi-albon was from Beth-arabah near the Jordan valley; Azmaveth from Bahurim, the village of Shimei.

f.g: Probably from Bahurim (2 Samuel 16:5), with two letters reversed.

chapters.n: Eliahba came from Shaalbim, a town once held by the Amorites. The sons of Jashen and Jonathan follow.

f.g: From Shaalbim, in the territory of Dan.

chapters.n: Shammah the Hararite (perhaps the father of Jonathan) and Ahiam come from the hill country.

f.g: Perhaps related to the Shammah of the Three, or the same man.

chapters.n: Eliphelet’s family came from Maacah, an Aramean region. Eliam, son of Ahithophel, may be the father of Bath-sheba — which would make the betrayal of her husband and the later rebellion of her grandfather all the more tangled.
Hezrai came from Carmel in Judah, the home of Nabal and Abigail; Paarai from Arab, another town in Judah’s hill country.
Igal came from Zobah, an Aramean kingdom David had defeated, and Bani from the tribe of Gad east of the Jordan. David’s army included former enemies.
Zelek was an Ammonite, and Naharai came from Beeroth — the town of Ish-bosheth’s murderers. He served as Joab’s armor-bearer.
Ira and Gareb were Ithrites, a clan from the area of Kirjath-jearim, where the ark had once rested.

The list ends with a sobering name: Uriah the Hittite, the loyal warrior David betrayed. Placing him last makes readers remember David’s sin even while honoring his heroes. The total of thirty-seven includes the leaders named earlier.

f.g: The Thirty plus the Three, Abishai, Benaiah, and probably Joab as commander.

chapters.n: The book closes with a census that brings judgment. Here the Lord is said to “move” David; the parallel account in 1 Chronicles says Satan provoked him. Scripture often describes God as the ultimate cause of what He permits.

f.g: Take a census, likely for military conscription or taxation.

chapters.n: David orders Joab to count all the fighting men from Dan in the north to Beer-sheba in the south. His motive seems to be pride in his own strength rather than trust in God.

f.g: The whole country, north to south.

f.w: that I may know the number of the people

chapters.n: Even Joab objects: may God multiply Israel a hundred times — but why does the king want to count them? He senses this is wrong.

f.w: why doth my lord the king delight in this thing?

chapters.n: The king overrules Joab and the army officers, and they set out to take the census.

f.g: Overruled.

chapters.n: The census-takers begin east of the Jordan, at Aroer by the Arnon gorge in the south, and move north toward Jazer.

f.g: A town on the Arnon River, Israel’s southern border east of the Jordan.

chapters.n: They continue through Gilead and up to Dan and the region near Sidon in the far north.

f.g: An unknown place; the text may be damaged here.
Sidon, a Phoenician city on the coast.

chapters.n: They go to the fortress of Tyre and the Canaanite and Hivite cities, then south through Judah to Beer-sheba.

f.g: One of the peoples living in Canaan before Israel.

chapters.n: The census takes nearly ten months to complete.
Joab reports 800,000 fighting men in Israel and 500,000 in Judah. (1 Chronicles 21:5 gives different figures, perhaps counting differently.)
Afterward David’s conscience strikes him. He confesses that he has sinned greatly and acted foolishly, and he asks God to take away his guilt. His quick, honest repentance is a mark of his character.

f.g: His conscience troubled him.

chapters.n: The next morning, the Lord gives a message to Gad, David’s prophet.

f.g: A prophet who sees by revelation.

chapters.n: God offers David a choice of three consequences.
The choices: years of famine, three months fleeing from enemies, or three days of plague. David must decide what answer to send back.

f.g: 1 Chronicles 21:12 reads “three years,” which matches the pattern of three.
A deadly epidemic or plague.

chapters.n: David chooses to fall into the hands of the Lord, trusting His great mercy, rather than the hands of men. Even in judgment, he knows God is more merciful than people.

f.g: A terrible dilemma; great distress.

chapters.n: The plague strikes, and seventy thousand people die across the land. The king’s sin affects the whole nation.

f.g: The appointed end of the three days; or perhaps the time of the evening sacrifice.

chapters.n: As the destroying angel reaches out over Jerusalem, the Lord relents and stops him. The angel stands by the threshing floor of Araunah — a location that will become sacred.

f.w: the LORD repented him of the evil
f.g: The Lord relented from the calamity — He chose mercy. “Evil” here means disaster, not sin.
Called Ornan in 1 Chronicles 21:15; a Jebusite who owned land in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Seeing the angel, David pleads for his people: he is the one who sinned; what have these sheep done? Let the punishment fall on him and his family. Like a true shepherd, he offers himself for the flock.

f.w: these sheep, what have they done?

chapters.n: Gad tells David to build an altar on Araunah’s threshing floor.
David obeys the Lord’s command through the prophet.
Araunah sees the king coming and bows to the ground before him.
David explains he has come to buy the threshing floor to build an altar so the plague will stop.

f.g: Stayed = stopped.

chapters.n: Araunah generously offers everything for free: the floor, oxen for sacrifice, and the wooden threshing sledges and yokes for firewood.

f.g: Heavy wooden sledges dragged over grain to thresh it.

chapters.n: Araunah gives like a king and prays that God will accept David’s offering.

f.g: Generously, royally; or possibly “O king.”

chapters.n: David refuses: he will not offer to God something that costs him nothing. True sacrifice must cost the giver. He pays fifty shekels of silver.

f.w: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing

f.g: Chronicles says 600 shekels of gold, perhaps for the whole site.

chapters.n: David builds the altar and offers sacrifices, and the Lord hears the prayer for the land; the plague stops. This very site would become the place where Solomon built the temple — on Mount Moriah, where Abraham once offered Isaac. Sacrifice and mercy meet there, pointing to the atoning sacrifice of Christ.

f.w: David built there an altar unto the LORD

f.g: The Lord responded to prayer.
